```js
    name: '2',
    prefix: '/',
    suffix: '',
```

If you use the `buffered: true` flag with `PerformanceObserver`, then you shouldn't need to wait until load, nor should you need to use the performance timeline at all (i.e. `performance.getEntriesByType()`).

And since Chrome/Chromium is the only browser to support paint timing, then you might as well just use the buffered flag (supported since M77) as shown in this example (note the use of `type` instead of `entryTypes`): https://web.dev/fcp/#measure-fcp-in-javascript

Also, as per our conversation, you'll probably want to wrap this in a try/catch to prevent an error in Safari ([this issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/web.dev/issues/2078) tracks updating the web.dev examples to account for the Safari error issue).

The original loader implementation from built-in CSS used a wrapped expression to evaluate whether to include `getClientStyleLoader()`:

```
ctx.isClient &&
  getClientStyleLoader({
    isDevelopment: ctx.isDevelopment,
    assetPrefix: ctx.assetPrefix,
  }),
```

This had to be filtered and use TS `as` in order to compile.

At: https://github.com/zeit/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/build/webpack/config/blocks/css/index.ts#L215

The `unshift()` allows you to avoid both. I can mimic the original implementation if desired.

- `foo` is the branch name, and `bar/1-navigate-between-pages` is the directory name

If we'd like to fix this existing bug, I'd be happy to send a different PR. I like to keep side-effects of a PR to a minimum.

body:
Thank you for asking. It's necessary for SSR to pass a resolver context to resolver functions. For SSR, it:

0. Starts from `WithApollo.getInitialProps`
1. Creates a resolver context from `req` and `res`
2. Initializes an apollo client instance with [`SchemaLink`](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/11681/files#diff-52c0088e3df4611902ee3b5f59a4a97dR196) with the resolver context
3. Executes `getDataFromTree`, which leads the apollo client to...
4. Pass the resolver context to [resolver functions as the 3rd argument](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/11681/files#diff-682d12e5f9468d1190b78c5c58a34533R5)

To pass a resolver context to resolver functions, we have to take care of two paths.

1. One for an  HTTP request to the GraphQL server (it's in `pages/api/graphql.ts`)
1. Another for SSR, done by `SchemaLink` that allows us to resolve GraphQL query without calling HTTP request.

The above code covers the case no. 2.

As you know, both paths run on the server-side, so here we have to get off client-side execution.

body:
Since Next doesn't support streaming, the only benefit of the "default approach" is that it works out of the box. It doesn't support certain selectors and style tags outside of head aren't valid HTML and may cause other issues (https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1605#issuecomment-235956455 and https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1605#issuecomment-277826129).

Having said that, I'm not recommending one approach over the other. I just updated an already existing example.

So, the attack you're guarding against with createScriptUrl is an untrusted/malicious URL, which can execute arbitrary code (e.g. by loading a script from a hostile origin that exfiltrates user data, mines bitcoins, etc)

It looks like you construct the URLs in two places, at line 263 and line 103. If you are confident that the data used to construct those URLs can't come from untrusted sources, then you could have a createScriptURL function that just returns its argument, and call policy.createScriptUrl there (with comments about your assumptions).

Then, because policy isn't exported, you and your users can reduce the amount of code that needs to be subject to careful security review to just those where the policy is used in this file.

body:
Without this specific change, babel-loader won't transpile files from the mono repo which resolve outside of the next app directory through the `paths` config.

This is particularly important in the case of the example repository I provided which has the following structure:
```
.
└── packages
    ├── bar
    ├── baz
    │   └── src
    ├── foo
    └── web-app
```
In this example when running `yarn --cwd packages/web-app next build`:
`dir` is the directory where `next.config.js` is, which resolves to `./packages/web-app`.
using this as include, prevents babel-loader from transpiling files in `./packages/bar`,`./packages/foo` and `./packages/baz`. Thus when they are resolved through the `paths` configuration in tsconfig, webpack will try to load them directly without transpilation.

author: timneutkens

body:
That's a valid concern:

> I'm not entirely sure it's the correct behavior given that other packages in a repo are pretty much outside of the scope of Next.js and suddenly compiling them could be an issue...

## Seems to require explicit opt-in

It is worth noting that by default nothing outside the Next root will be compiled - when you set up your project and start using typescript, the generated `tsconfig.json` does not include a `baseUrl`; so compilation will be limited to the Next folder.

A developer has to make a very explicit change to modify the `baseUrl`.

I'm trying to think why would anyone do this (modify baseUrl Next's `tsconfig`, either directly or through `extends`), if their intent is not to have code outside the Next folder compiled. But I cannot, for now at least, see this happening.

## Some background on mono-repos

I'm probably not the common Next user as I've been using Next nearly exclusively with mono-repos (either `docs` or `site`). And these have been either JS or TS.

You always do the same thing:

- You need to add the aliases to the webpack config where:
  - I always used my own bespoke alias resolver as you also often also need it for eslint and babel
  - then also config `baseUrl/paths`  in `tsconfig.json` to keep VScode happy
- Add `next-transpile-modules` so the other packages get compiled and bundled.

Our aliases would point to the `src` folder of the various packages, because Next would be there way before packages even get built into their own dist and published. Next builds for us are always apps/sites - a deployable rather than published package - you want everything bundled (at least everything in the mono-repo, some `node_modules` may flagged as externals, and loaded via `unpkg.com`) .

For us, we always want other packages bundled in both development and production builds - the whole point was that Next would build and bundle the source of other packages. It is an 'integration hub' if you wish.

Then there could be some extra effort in ensuring that when you build each package, aliases are not in force and one package does not bundle the other.

# What other use case then?

So I think there are two questions to be answered:

- When could a developer explicitly modify `baseUrl` yet not wish for anything under that `baseUrl` be complied?
- How could a developer mistakenly modify `baseUrl`?
author: Izhaki

body:
Although it's rather obvious, it is worth pointing out that with this change 2 things need to happen in order for stuff outside the Next project root to be compiled and bundled:

- The developer needs to explicitly set `baseUrl`.
- The developer has to import something from either outside the the Next root, or use an explicitly-set alias that points outside the Next root and use it.

So seems to me that there are already sufficient guards in place.

Babel works in a way that it takes the input, parses it, and then applies transforms to that parsed input. The input would be the result of the previous loader, so the code itself would not change in most cases. It's not related to optimizations 👍

`.js` files could also be in the dependency graph without being passed through Babel if you just import them, e.g. `import MyLib from '../other-package/my-lib.js'`. This change would affect that if the root tsconfig already had a `baseUrl`

body:
For security reasons an absolute URL must unfortunately be specified manually.

* It's possible to grab the hostname from the request object (e.g. `req.host`) but that is supplied by the client and can't be trusted.
* You can infer the URL of the instance but it's impossible to guess the intended canonical URL of an instance and that's important for OAuth integration to work

   e.g. callback URLs at `www.example.com` and `example.com` are not the same as far most OAuth providers are concerned - typically it has to match exactly whatever you have told them the URL of your site is.
author: iaincollins

Hey @timneutkens 😄

I did an event emitter for the router events, refer to https://codesandbox.io/s/nextjs-events-2in1n?file=/src/index.ts:785-1124

But I'm having some doubts in order to implement it with the current ``mitt`` 

In order to type the handlers, we should pass a map type as a generic. 
```
interface Mitt<T extends RouterEventMap> {
  on<K extends RouterEventKey<RouterEventMap>>(
    type: K,
    handler: RouterEventHandler<K>
  ): void;
  off<K extends RouterEventKey<RouterEventMap>>(
    type: K,
    handler: RouterEventHandler<K>
  ): void;
  emit<K extends RouterEventKey<RouterEventMap>>(type: K, ...evts: T[K]): void;
}
```

But the ``mitt`` function it's being used in two places: 

Inside of the ``router.ts``: 
```
  static events = mitt<RouterEvent, (url: string) => void>()
```

Inside of the class ``ServerRouter``: 

```
  static events = mitt<string>()
```

The generic being passed to the ``mitt`` function above it's just a string, so there are two different cases. 

How can we pass the ``RouterEventMap`` as a generic for the router emitter and a ``string`` as a generic for the ``ServerRouter`` events emitter?

author: leerob

body:
Here's a proposal:

---

Here's some information to help you decide on using use `next-auth` or `next-iron-session`:

`next-auth` combines sessions, authentication providers (GitHub, Apple and 20+) and user accounts (if you need it) into a single package. Session data can be stored on your server (database) or on the clients (JWT/JWE).

Example usage: You want to add a GitHub login, have it create user accounts and use JWTs as sessions, use `next-auth`.

`next-iron-session` provides `req.session.set/get/unset/save/destroy` methods and that's it. The session data is encrypted and stored on the client as secured, http-only and same-site:lax cookies.

Example usage: You want sessions helpers you can plug wherever you want, and a small API.

---

Do you want me to add this as a suggestion to your document via GitHub?

Side note: next-auth definitely looks like a more complete solution than next-iron-session. But they have different goals and public.

For example, **I** get "scared" the more options I see in a library. Because it usually means it will get into my way at some point.

Others will get scared by the scarcity of packages like next-iron-session, wondering how they could use that to build their GitHub OAuth login for their app.

Let me know!

It's because the paths above are symlinks that after being resolved don't respect anymore the regex  /node_modules[/\\].*\.js$/


It was explained in the commit message

```
Ensure certain 'next/*' pkgs get externalized on the server

- 'next/amp'
- 'next/config'
- 'next/dynamic'
- 'next/head'

e2e tests were failing prior to this change because e.g.

    next.js/node_modules/next/dynamic.js

is a symlink to

    next.js/packages/next/dynamic.js

So the

    if (isNextExternal || res.match(/node_modules[/\\].*\.js$/)) {

condition was not being met (the regex no longer matched).

By making sure we have a guard at the top to externalize these packages,
we avoid this issue.
```

body:
If I remember correctly, the Promise to load the specific module would reject. Which should be similar to the current fallback solution. Maybe with a check to see if the requested locale is part of the list of supported locales to short-circuit the detection.

So far, I did not encounter this issue at runtime, as I'm usually having an enum-type object upstream that limits the selection so only known values are inputs of the function. In this case I would add an `supportedLocales.includes(locale)` type of check to make sure, only supported locales are loaded.
That check could be powered by `require.context` to get the list of supported locales directly from the available locales.
author: thuringia

body: Yeah ￼￼￼￼my concern is maintaining supportedLocales separately. Does require.context work in client side though?
author: longlho

body: `require.context` will be resolved at build time. It works client-side via the webpack runtime but it doesn't recognize new files during runtime, as it is based on the layout of the file tree at build.
author: thuringia

body:
On the client it is basically a specially prepared version of `require`.
I have successfully used it to load components dynamically based on runtime config like CMS-content. So I'm confident this works, at least for this case here.
As a small bonus, we can use the same code to load messages etc. during development
author: thuringia

body: maybe @lfades can advise here from a next.js perspective. IMO relying on `require` is basically relying on `webpack` implementation details instead of spec'ed runtime environment (such as ECMA262 or such). Different runtimes can deal with `require` differently (e.g `jest` does module resolution in a custom manner...) so it's fairly unstable. TBH idk what `next`'s guarantee of this behavior is since it is undocumented.

author: remorses

body:
That's fair.

I'm more worried about cases where a dependency is used by the Next.js app under test, but is missing from the pnpm `node_modules` tree.

For example, if we forget to install `react` or another peer dependency, then it will instead be imported from the monorepo `node_modules`.

A more likely scenario is that a dependency is mistakenly omitted from the `next` package's dependencies list, e.g. https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/8344 (this example is for "next-server", but the same could apply to "next"). We want this to cause the pnpm integration test to fail, but if it's not isolated from the monorepo `node_modules`, then the test will pass.

We can't use React to render into the head as you'd have to nest the rendering in an element and `<head>` needs tags to be inserted at the top level of the tag. Hence why it's using a custom renderer that does not support custom react components. 

It's documented as part of the `next/head` documentation:

> title, meta or any other elements (e.g. script) need to be contained as direct children of the Head element, or wrapped into maximum one level of <React.Fragment> or arrays—otherwise the tags won't be correctly picked up on client-side navigations.

https://nextjs.org/docs/api-reference/next/head

The legacy next-css package doesn't use `require.resolve` to access its loaders, which leaves it vulnerable when the hoisting changes slightly. In this case, it caused crashes because the `css-loader` version hoisted to the top wasn't exactly the same one as the one in dependency.

This rewrite is invalid, dynamic route interpolation is meant to be a client-side feature as shown in the docs here https://nextjs.org/docs/routing/introduction#linking-to-dynamic-paths

For this rewrite to be valid it should map to the dynamic route providing all values in the destination and not the dynamic route itself. e.g. the destination here should be `/product/:itemId`

This is a good point. Just checked and it seems that only the "next" package is packed, not the other monorepo dependencies like `@next/polyfill-module`, `@next/react-dev-overlay`.

I pushed an change which packs `@next/env`, `@next/polyfill-module`, `@next/react-dev-overlay`, and `@next/react-refresh-utils` into tarballs too, and ensures they're installed upon running `pnpm install` by using a [pnpmfile.js hook](https://pnpm.js.org/en/pnpmfile).

This is the best I could come up with to make the install process as similar as possible to the real world (installing from a registry), without actually installing from a registry.

An even more correct pnpm test would involve publishing all of the monorepo packages to a local npm registry (maybe [verdaccio](https://github.com/verdaccio/verdaccio)?), then telling pnpm to install packages from there. Would something like this be preferred?

body:
`lazy` is after onload - basically we wait for all resources to be downloaded
`defer` is on hydration - here were start loading after prioritizing only 1P scripts

This difference may seem subtle but we've seen traces of apps where the onload can be significantly delayed because of cascading requests. So onload and onHydration can have a large time delta in terms of when they trigger a script load.

The decision is also nuanced depending on the type of app, what resources they prioritize, what type of 3P scripts they load etc. **So we wanted more options initially to experiment and then determine the right defaults.**

A potential example of using `lazy` vs `defer` is we were experimenting with loading GTM with `lazy` and something like Social login/video player with `defer` (because onHydration the buttons become interactive and you don't want to wait for images to load)

body:
I haven't checked that yet, but what I did try is using webpack 5 and using async/await in the regular component code in `_app`. These statements were changed to ES5 as expected, but only the top-level await code resulted in native async/await code.

That made me wondering if top-level await only works with native async/await but I'd assume there should be some way for webpack to resolve the modules with promises and calling `then`.

As far as I understand the build chain, the user-land async/await code is compiled with Babel and then provided to webpack. But for top-level await code Babel doesn't attempt to transform it, since it needs to rely on the bundler to do this. The bundler chooses to turn it into native async/await which happens to break in IE11.

So I'm wondering if this is really a webpack issue, as I guess you wouldn't want to run babel again on the bundle code that webpack has produced.

body:
I agree it's a bit confusing, it caught me off guard as well.

What I get from it is that there are two different forms of caching: on the process hosting NextJS (server) and browser (client) side.

Here, the client side is instructed to always check if there's a newer version of the image available. Which is necessary with the introduction of etags to allow the NextJS process to invalidate images at any time.

On the server side, NextJS has its own cache for the generated images. The cached image will be served according to the `max-age` header value when retrieving the image, defaulting to 60 seconds if the header was not supplied.

That was a great question. 👍 The Contentful Images API is not upscaling and keeps the max uploaded image dimensions even when `w` is greater than the dimension.

Example:

- [original image](https://images.ctfassets.net/f20lfrunubsq/6E6lO4YbOiZJsD48z5ks6/8eb86af58492e4915fe816a478d20a20/Screenshot_2020-08-30_at_18.43.36.png) – 420k in size with 1378 × 832

author: stefanjudis

body: @styfle be sure to pass a quality parameter `q` when you are delivering images via Contentful's Images API; the quality is set to 100% without it, resulting in much larger images. This is true of WebP and JPG. I recommend experimenting with `q` values from 30-70.

body:
This is a common problem with listening on socket files. If the program doesn't close cleanly, it's very common to leave socket files around. There are 2 common ways to deal with this that are not mutually exclusive, afaik:
1. Use process init script to check/cleanup existing sockets. Systemd's `RuntimeDirectory=` option effectively does this by removing and recreating the directory on ever execution. By putting a socket file in there, you're guaranteed to never run into `EADDRINUSE`.
2. If you detect/catch this error, test the socket file for if it's still connectable with a client socket. If it's not connectable, the server that created the socket file is probably dead. So you can remove the socket file and try again. If it is connectable, close the connection and throw the original `EADDRINUSE`.

body:
So I did not test it yet, but I am pretty sure this is going to announce the document’s title twice. Once from `RouteAnnouncer`, since it’s an assertive live region, and then a second time when focusing the document’s main title. 

I’m not entirely certain, but it feels like you are mixing two approaches here:

1. **Focusing the main heading.** Upon route change, and provided you can guarantee there will be a `<h1>` element regardless of state such as loading, move the focus to the main heading. As a result, its content will be announced.

2. **Announcing the page title.** If the presence of a `<h1>` cannot be guaranteed for any reason (because left to the implementor who might not know, or because depending on loading states for instance), move the focus to a visually hidden node as `<body>`’s first child containing the new document title (which doesn‘t have to be a region whatsoever).

Both are equally good as far as I know. The main difference is where the focus ends up being. In the first approach, the focus is moved to the main page title, which could be anywhere in the page, really. Some sites have it in the title, some have it in the main container, some have it after the navigation, some before… In the second case, the focus is consistently moved at the top of the body (where the `RouteAnnouncer` DOM node lives), just like a regular `href` link would after a page load.

Because you appear to be essentially doing both, I am pretty certain this will announce the document’s main title twice, which is probably not what you want. I might be entirely mistaken though, so feel free to correct me. :)

**Edit:** a little [more information in that article](https://kittygiraudel.com/2020/01/15/accessible-title-in-a-single-page-react-application/).

**Edit 2:** Finding the first `<h1>` element on the page could lead to issues if a hidden dialog with a `<h1>` element is being rendered high up the body element. That heading will be queried because it’s the first, but attempting to focus it would not work because it is within a hidden dialog.

body:
Hey! Thank you so much for taking the time to look at this, and more importantly, for the feedback! ❤️

I think your judgement is 100% valid. The intent here was to bring focus to the most important part of the page; however, this makes quite a few assumptions about the user's site. For example, the heading might be visually hidden. This alone makes me think that, while focusing on the top-most heading might be helpful for many sites, just focusing on the body will be best. So I will remove the logic for querying the header for the purpose of focusing.

The following is probably a moot point, but because the `<RouteAnnouncer />` uses `aria-live="assertive"`, the screen reader is expected to stop what it's doing and announce the new page name. Since the focus & route announcement happen at the same time, most screen readers will give priority to the `<RouteAnnouncer />` and not announce the focused element. I've tested this on a few screen readers.

Look out for a commit soon with this change 😉

```suggestion
	// directory with a tailing slash
```

```diff
+tempDir=$(mktemp -d)
+trap 'rm -rf -- "$tempDir"' EXIT

 for testCase in "${testCases[@]}"
 do
-  testTarget=$(mktemp -d)
+  testTarget="$tempDir/$testCase"
+
+  mkdir -p "$testTarget"
```

body: That's the issue: you can't because functions are not JSONable, and what Next abstracts from us is basically a REST call (or something). But you don't have to right? `fetchMore` is only sugar for passing just a cursor (and Apollo will fill the rest of the vars with whatever was there before). If you hydrate on the first render on the client side, you should still be perfectly able to fetch the cursor from your fetched data and pass it to `fetchMore`. Really the only difference is that the first render will have cached Apollo Client data. This is the only connecting between Apollo and Next (with SSR). You fill the cache with whatever arbitrary data you want (most of the times, the first data the client will need). From the pages side, none of this matters, they just do whatever queries they need, and Apollo will have them in cache, they code stays the same. The only issue here (I think) is how to hydrate this state, and IMO it can be done with `useApolloClient` (get the client, hydrate data, etc etc), right before you `useQuery`. Of course you can abstract this away with a custom hook to reuse between pages. Something like `useHydratedQuery`.

> yarn install --production is close, but it does a few things prune doesn't. It's a little annoying to have to build native modules twice in a CI pipeline just to prune. You can prevent rebuilding packages that already exist in cache with the --ignore-scripts flag. Additionally, prune doesn't check npm registry, so add --prefer-offline.
>
> So, yarn install --production --ignore-scripts --prefer-offline == npm prune --productio

body:
Looking back at it, I think the logic might be a little backwards here.

In my opinion, we should use the `document.title` first if available, since this is what would happen in a non-SPA scenario upon page change. And if we do not have a page title, we should use the `h1` (if any, of course). Right now it will announce the content of the `h1`, despite having a perfectly clean `document.title`, which I think is not the best experience.

Taking the home page of the [Gorillas website](https://gorillas.io/en) as an example: the page title is “Home | Gorillas” while the `h1` is “Groceries delivered in 10 minutes”. Navigating to the home page should announce “Home | Gorillas”, not the baseline (or catch phrase, or whatever we want to name it). And while in many cases, the `h1` and the `document.title` would be in sync, I believe this is not always the case. In a case like this, we also don’t want the `h1` to just contain “Home.”

Pinging @kyleboss who authored the original PR for opinions. :)

Edit: I’m happy opening an issue/PR if you think this is a valid concern.

Thanks for taking the time to open a PR, in general we recommend opening a RFC first to avoid situations where a PR will not be merged and work could have been avoided.

As said in multiple other threads we're not planning to add support for Less to Next.js. It's not used by a large percentage of apps (approximately 4,75%) and would have to be maintained long-term. For comparison Sass is used by 29.79%, tailwind by 15.34%, antd by 9,08%. It also seems that Less is not actively being worked on in comparison to Sass. Adding Less support would make optimizations like https://twitter.com/shuding_/status/1378086219708473344 significantly more difficult as it would be yet another constraint to account for.

body:
Usually mongoose is used like this:

```js
import mongoose from 'mongoose'

mongoose.//
```

The first time the connection is created it will be fine, but when re-used the mongoose connections array won't be touched, and instead it will work if used directly from the result of this function call (`dbConnect`).

Let's make it so `mongoose.connections` is updated if the connection is re-used. You would use `mongoose.createConnection`  instead of `connect` for this case.

Use the `lastModified` filesystem timestamp from the filesystem cache when refreshing the `LRUCache` content in `IncrementalCache.get`.

body:
As someone trying to understand how the Next.js custom Express setup works, I have some questions:

If the `server.get()` path handlers are not needed here, does that mean the `server.all()` handler will just know how to handle all the paths defined in [pages](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/243472f34d58e516c8980eadccb276ff85611f9f/examples/custom-server-express/pages/index.js#L7-L12)? So I'm assuming we can just define API endpoints here that Express needs to handle and all the application path routing will just work.

If yes, then what's the point of all the `app.render` in the [documentation example](https://nextjs.org/docs/advanced-features/custom-server)? Shouldn't that only be done when file-system routing is disabled? Having it in the basic example makes it look like it's necessary to define all the path handlers.

I'm also confused about what the `query` parameter is and how and when it is supposed to be used. In the lines deleted here, we were using `req.query` and that worked fine. But the documentation example shows that `query` should be taken from the result of `parse(req.url, true)` and then passed to the `app.render`. Can't find any explanation of what `query` parameter is exactly supposed to be and why does `app.render` need it.

I'd expect the documentation/examples to have a mention of:
- Where do the express middlewares fit here?
- Is it necessary to define path handlers for every route of the application?
- Where are the response headers supposed to be in a custom server with Next.js? Will express keep handling the headers for every page request or will Next.js headers override that functionality? Are there any conflicts between the two?

Understandably, these questions could be directed to Discussions or StackOverflow but it'd be great if it's possible to figure these answers out from the documentation.

body:
Reading the files directly from fs is probably not the best idea.

A loader could have modified the source code after filesystem. Or it could be transpiled from a language nft doesn't understand.

There is a `NormalModule.originalSource()` function which gives you the source code for a module after loader processing. That's in a language webpack understands, so either javascript, or something else you can ignore. Best check `Module.type` for `javascript/*` to only process JS code.

Note that some modules might not end up at all in the output, so best use the list of chunks from `createTraceAssets` and grab all modules from there, de-duplicate them, analyse them with nft for more references, merge and cache the results per chunk and add them to the analysis data while iterating over the chunks.

The current `<script>` and `<Script>` have the same properties due to the `extends ScriptHTMLAttributes` here.

If for some reason there are props missing, its best to get this changed upstream in the `ScriptHTMLAttributes` interface via `@types/react`

body:
Rust does not have an out-of-the-box cross compile mechanism, which `Go` and `Zig` provided. So it's really hard to build all platform/cpu targets on one system. The root cause of Rust's lack of a cross compile mechanism is that Rust relies on the `GCC` toolchain for the Link phase of compilation. And the GCC toolchain usually looks for the appropriate C dependencies on the host (glibc/musl-libc) for the system call on ***target*** platform/cpu. The toolchain and `C dependencies` must be set up properly on your host machine if you want cross compile Rust program.

[package-template](https://github.com/napi-rs/package-template) is the template project I set up for napi-rs users to build multi platform targets addons smoothly. And I've set up the cross build matrix and toolchain in it for the most used platforms: https://github.com/napi-rs/package-template/blob/main/.github/workflows/CI.yaml#L17-L198
The Docker images and used in this project is maintained by `napi-rs`, and tested by many projects.

If you have any questions about cross compile or `napi-rs`, feel free to contact with me! I'm willing to help here 🚀

body:
There are a lot of knobs to turn here.

The default [`maxSockets`](
https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#http_new_agent_options) and [`maxTotalSockets`](
https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#http_new_agent_options) are set to Infinity. So configuring these wouldn't really increase performance but might improve stability.

Using `socket.setNoDelay()` seems like it could improve performance in some cases, but the default delayed behavior (Nagles Algorithm) already "optimizes throughput at the expense of latency".

Finally, theres [`scheduling`](https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#http_new_agent_options) that was actually changed in Node.js 15.6.0 from FIFO to LIFO in https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/36685

body:
It's better to use `Id` from `swc_ecmascript::utils`.
See: https://docs.rs/swc_ecma_utils/0.41.0/swc_ecma_utils/ident/type.Id.html

SWC handles scoping via metadata in `span.ctxt` of `Ident` and `Id` consists of `(Ident.sym, Ident.span.ctxt)`.
Such metadata is added by [`resolver`](https://docs.rs/swc_ecma_transforms/0.63.0/swc_ecma_transforms/resolver/fn.resolver_with_mark.html) and in future, custom passes invoked after applying resolver, so that custom passes can use such metadata for distinguishing identifiers.

body:
This will panic if the user does not pass any argument to this call.

There are several ways for handling this error.

react jsx pass of swc reports error via `swc_emca_utils::HANDLER`, like https://github.com/swc-project/swc/blob/48bc26d3c93e64174b3d1cd269205a98b1581a0c/ecmascript/transforms/react/src/jsx/mod.rs#L411-L423
This will print a nice-looikng error on stderr, as it's configured while creating `swc_common::Handler`. (See https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/d368f76b4dff84a2db46ee50a09ae29003f11b30/packages/next/build/swc/src/lib.rs#L56-L61)

You can also store the error in the struct (`NextDynamicPatcher `), and check for it after applying transforms. You can panic or pass error to napi task defined at https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/d368f76b4dff84a2db46ee50a09ae29003f11b30/packages/next/build/swc/src/transform.rs#L66-L79
This seems unpractical to me.

Alternatively, you can simply panic and it will be an exception for javascript.

@styfle From my understanding, that test was passing before because filenames with multiple dots didn't work, as the code considered the file would have a single dot only (the file extension). So if you had `file.name.with.dots.png` it'd return only `file.png`.

I'm not sure if we need more updates to the integration specs. It seems it tests that when sending a request with a filename in query params, its response has the same name and the optimized extension on the `'Content-Disposition'` response header.

I've added some unit specs covering the case [here](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/2b0ab38c9d423948bbfe19c940ac13af6005ee1f/test/unit/image-optimizer/get-file-name-with-extension.test.ts).

```suggestion
# Invalid Project Directory Casing

#### Why This Error Occurred

When starting Next.js, the current directory is a different casing than the actual directory on your filesystem. This can cause files to resolve inconsistently.

This can occur when using a case-insensitive filesystem. For example, opening PowerShell on Windows navigating to `cd path/to/myproject` instead of `cd path/to/MyProject`.

#### Possible Ways to Fix It

Ensure the casing for the current working directory matches the actual case of the real directory. Use a terminal that enforces case-sensitivity.

### Useful Links

- [Next.js CLI documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/api-reference/cli)
- [Case sensitivity in filesystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_sensitivity#In_filesystems)
```

body:
My concern here is all those WASM modules will always be initialized immediately. Previously with `() => resize.default(fsp.readFile(pathify(resizeWasm)))`, they were only initialized lazily.

For example if the resize processor isn't used, `squoosh_resize_bg.wasm` will **still** be loaded in this worker. Since the workers are keyed by the task it handles: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/92c2dd4971c8ff04ecdc0ad5948a58c95391376c/packages/next/server/lib/squoosh/main.ts#L16-L25

Previously, it ensures that 1 worker only loads and handles 1 type of task, for example: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/92c2dd4971c8ff04ecdc0ad5948a58c95391376c/packages/next/server/lib/squoosh/main.ts#L64

This worker has only loaded the `encodeJpeg` related WASM module inside. And tasks of `encodeJpeg` will always be assigned to this same worker. That ensures that we don't allocate the memory for every WASM module inside every worker.
author: shuding

body:
This is generally OK I think (3. in #23565). Removing it will not leak more memory, but it won't clean up the allocated memory for the finished task. When a new task arrives, the memory will still get released and new memory is allocated for the new task. So the behavior is basically:
- Current canary: new task (100MB↑), GC (100MB↓), new task (100MB↑), GC (100MB↓), ...
- With this PR: new task (100MB↑), new task (unchanged), new task (unchanged), ...

For long-running servers, it's definitely ideal to keep this logic though (or fix it in the upstream lib).

```suggestion
When using URL imports, Next.js will create a lockfile in the `next.lock` directory.
This directory is intended to be committed to git and should not be included in your `.gitignore` file.

- When running `next dev`, Next.js will download and add all newly discovered URL Imports to your lockfile.
- When running `next build`,  Next.js will use only the lockfile to build the application for production.

Typically, no network requests are needed and any outdated lockfile will cause the build to fail.
One exception is resources that respond with `Cache-Control: no-cache`.
These resources will have a `no-cache` entry in the lockfile and will always be fetched from the network on each build.
```

body:
Can we use `crypto.randomUUID()` and fallback to `uuid()` if it doesn't exist?

That way we can remove the `uuid` package in the future when we drop Node.js 12 support.

https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html#cryptorandomuuidoptions
author: styfle

body:
I'm not convinced about this one @styfle . The API for `randomUUID` was introduced in Node 15 and types are not currently updated for that. In fact, `@types/node` are not listed at all in the package so we'd have to add them to a certain version (maybe latest?).

That said, if we add types for version that includes `randomUUID`, we will get some type deprecations for other APIs we use but are deprecated for recent node versions, and other types APIs that might not be available in the running version.

Considering all of this, do you think we should update it in this PR? We can also remove fallbacks / polyfills once we deprecate old Node versions.

```suggestion
Client-side data fetching is useful when your page doesn't require SEO indexing, when you don't need to pre-render your data, or when the content of your pages needs to update frequently. Unlike the server-side rendering APIs, you can use client-side data fetching at the component level.
```

body:
```suggestion
If done at the page level, the data is fetched at runtime, and the content of the page is updated as the data changes. When used at the component level, the data is fetched at the time of the component mount, and the content of the component is updated as the data changes.
```

body:
```suggestion
You should use `getServerSideProps` only if you need to pre-render a page whose data must be fetched at request time. [Time to First Byte (TTFB)](/learn/seo/web-performance) will be higher than [`getStaticProps`](/docs/basic-features/data-fetching/getStaticProps.md) because the server must compute the result on every request, and the result can only be cached by a CDN using `cache-control` headers (which could require extra configuration).
```

TTFB is a metric value that can be low or high, not slow.
author: balazsorban44

body:
```suggestion
- When you request this page on client-side page transitions through [`next/link`](/docs/api-reference/next/link.md) or [`next/router`](/docs/api-reference/next/router.md), Next.js sends an API request to the server, which runs `getServerSideProps`. It’ll return JSON that contains the result of running `getServerSideProps`, and the `JSON` will be used to render the page. All this work will be handled automatically by Next.js, so you don’t need to do anything extra as long as you have `getServerSideProps` defined
```

body:
Why was this change made?

It means that a middleware cannot longer set headers without breaking the middleware chain as we have below:

```js
        if (!result.response.headers.has('x-middleware-next')) {
          break
        }
```

This will break some of the examples, like [this one](https://github.com/vercel/examples/blob/30577906af4090c2031b8f18e4ecd0fcf6df1e65/edge-functions/ip-blocking-datadome/lib/datadome.ts#L133).

It also means that a middleware cannot simply add a cookie and keep the rest as is. For example, you may want to add a `csrf` cookie if missing, but not break the middleware chain or return a custom `Response`.

body:
Ok. I understand your worries. Since you're much more into NextJS, I'd say you can just close this PR, if you think it's not worth it.

Let me one more time explain why I think it could be worth it:
- If you're using a `basePath` your assets and the `pages/index.ts` file are expected to be the entries to your app at the URL with its `basePath`.
- If you're using rewrite rules to your dev system for everything except for paths that are prefixed by the `basePath`, you'll find that opening the address printed without the `basePath` will be looking broken and this might confuse some devs.
- It increases the manual overhead, having to click on the link and then going to the URL bar, writing the `basePath` on my own each time, and finally reloading the page

Like I said, if this is sufficient, I totally understand your decision to close the PR :+1:

Thank you for being so responsive to me 🙂

```This strategy only works inside **\_document.js** and is designed to load scripts that is needed by the entire site```

Which of the following correct?

- Script will only load once on a page reload (SSR) and not during page transitions (CSR), but will load when any page is reloaded
- Script will load during page reload (SSR) and during client side transitions

I assume it's the first option, and if so - can we clarify that a bit here? Something along the lines of:

```suggestion
Scripts that load with the `beforeInteractive` strategy are injected into the initial HTML from the server and run before self-bundled JavaScript is executed. This strategy should be used for any critical scripts that need to be fetched and executed before any page becomes interactive. This strategy only works inside **\_document.js** and is designed to load scripts that is needed by the entire site (i.e. the script will load when any page in the application has been loaded server-side).
```

body:
When we made our preview mode demo we ran into issues where the chain of redirects that came from a different origin had the cookie missing. Example:
- Visit website https://example.com from Twitter
- https://example.com sets a cookie for `test-group: a` and does a redirect to `/home`
- Browser request to `https://example.com/home` has the cookie missing
- Manually refresh (F5), cookie is now there!

Chrome bug: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=696204

Trick we used to fix: https://github.com/vercel/preview-mode-demo/blob/master/src/pages/api/sameorigin/%5BsnapshotId%5D.tsx

---

tl;dr _should_ be fine if coming from same origin, but the **entire** redirect chain has to be same origin. This is particularly painful for links opened from link trackers (twitter/facebook/email campaigns) that redirect.

body:
Hi, so this statement is still accurate in that we don't send the `redirects` to the client to use them during resolving client-side navigations. The case where `redirects` can fail with `next/link` is when you have a `redirect` that should take priority over a client-side route like a `rewrite` or a page e.g. if we have a redirect `{ source: '/first', destination: '/somewhere' }` and then a page `pages/[slug].js` then `next/link` will navigate to `[slug]` since it matches. 

If a page or `rewrite` is not matched client-side then Next.js will do a hard navigation which will then trigger the redirect to apply server-side. 

Maybe we can tweak this note to make the above scenario where they won't take affect more clear

body:
@tbezman Sure! A developer changed the fragment or a query (added/changed field, etc), but didn't run the `relay-compiler`. When they refresh the page, the generated artifact for this file (.graphql.js file) won't contain the changes, this sometimes may lead to confusing situations, when developers may not see changes they are expecting on the screen.

To reduce the confusion, In the babel plugin we're comping the `md5` hash of the text inside `graphql` tag. And we're comparing this hash to the `hash` in the generated artifact (created by the compiler), if these hashes are different - we're showing a warning in the browser's console. When developers debug the outdated views, they may see the reason in the console.

```suggestion
You should use `getServerSideProps` only if you need to pre-render a page whose data must be fetched at request time. [Time to First Byte (TTFB)](/learn/seo/web-performance) will be higher than [`getStaticProps`](/docs/basic-features/data-fetching/get-static-props.md) because the server must compute the result on every request, and the result can only be cached by a CDN using `cache-control` headers (which could require extra configuration).
```

body:
```suggestion
When combined with [Incremental Static Regeneration](/docs/basic-features/data-fetching/incremental-static-regeneration.md), `getStaticProps` will run in the background while the stale page is being revalidated, and the fresh page served to the browser.

Because `getStaticProps` runs at build time, it does **not** have access to the incoming request (such as query parameters or `HTTP` headers) as it generates static `HTML`. If you need access to the request for your page, consider using [Middleware](/docs/middleware.md) in addition to `getStaticProps`.
```

body: So, the issue is that _router_ is a bit of a misnomer here. When used globally, it means "routing functions + a reference to the currently visible route." When used locally (via a React hook), it means "routing functions + the currently rendered route." The router context _should_ change for each tree IMO. Consider something like this: ```jsx function Foo() { const { query } = useRouter() return {JSON.stringify(query)} } ``` 1. If the context didn't change when `query` changed, how would `Foo` rerender? 2. If the value of `query` only pointed to the active route, how would we support `startTransition`, which renders the _next_ page concurrently in the background, and presumably wants the _new_ `query` value? My approach in #33875 is working on addressing this from this perspective, i.e. just creating a new public instance for each route/navigation, instead of generating a new one each time `AppContainer` is rerendered. The approach in this PR is probably fine to unblock for now, but I don't think it'll work for concurrent rendering.

```suggestion
Enabling streaming SSR means React renders your components into streams and the client continues receiving updates from these streams even after the initial SSR response is sent. author: gaearon
```

body:
The issue is that currently that would be a breaking change without an incremental upgrade path: your application using `next/dynamic` would break when upgrading to React 18 unless you add suspense boundaries first, but you can't add suspense boundaries until you upgrade to React 18. It also changes the semantics a bit, since pre-Suspense, the loading state is associated with the `next/dynamic` component, rather than the parent where the component is rendered.

Changing the default in the future is a possibility, but it's likely a major version away. Some shorter term options might be:
* If we could detect that we're rendering inside a `<Suspense>` boundary, we could assume you want the suspense behavior
* If we could somehow port the preloading behavior to `React.lazy`, we could push users toward that instead, when using React>=18

Both of these options would probably require some support in React though.

> Is the concern its not required in all pages?

Exactly. I was loading it in SSR *and* in CSR with the idea being that if there's no worker scripts on the initial page (`<script strategy="worker">`) but in a subsequent client-side transition; then load it only when necessary.

The snippet itself is just ~1KB though, so this was pretty unnecessary. I just removed this client-side logic completely. :)

> Maybe we can bundle it and save the extra RTT and justify loading it everytime

I did bundle it using `ncc` in the first iteration of the PR, but @adamdbradley (author of Partytown) provided some good feedback and mentioned that since it's still an experimental library—it might be better to allow users to install any version of the dependency themselves. In addition, the library's [publish size](https://packagephobia.com/result?p=%40builder.io%2Fpartytown) isn't trivial (328 KB) so it likely makes more sense for the user to install it only when needed.

body:
This is a highly wanted feature since `next/image` launch.

I think there's a misinterpretation between what `raw` means for users and what `raw` means for this PR.

What we, the users, need is a `raw` as in:

1. No **_forced_** NextJs styles
2. We need to be able to set `priority` and preload it if necessary
3. We want the blurry placeholder

We simply don't want the actual `layout` because it either bloat the DOM or messes up how we position the image in our designs.

At launch, the styles were even using `!important` to make sure we couldn't overwrite it... it was so bad some of us simply gave up on `next/image` altogether.

Personally, I completely rewrote the client-side `next/image` to be able to use it. Here's the Gist and there's a section that enumerates some improvements on the ideas of `next/image`: https://gist.github.com/TheThirdRace/7f270a786629f119b57d1b2227a4b113

I retained pretty much all your functionalities without using any `layout`. It shows that pretty much everything you've done was great, the only bad step was to tie in the `layout` as a **_forced_** option because that removed any flexibility and increased DOM bloating to the roof.
author: TheThirdRace

body:
`Insert the image element with no responsive behavior` is misleading here. Point in case, the very next column describe how it auto-adjust its source according to responsive space available.

I think it would be better to say `Insert the image element without any wrappers` or `without NextJs layouts applied` .

The "responsive" aspect you're referring to is more about NextJs layouts than what people are expecting "responsive" to mean in an image context. That's why I would leave that out of the description so nobody confuses `NextJs responsive layouts` with `responsive images`, which are 2 totally different things.
author: TheThirdRace

body: Technically, `objectFit` and `objectPosition` could easily be passed to the `style` attribute on the `` component when `layout === 'raw'`. With the current implementation, you're creating 2 methods to specify `objectFit` and `objectPosition`: 1. Pass the actual properties to the component 2. Pass some CSS in the `style` attribute This has some consequences: 1. The errors thrown creates frustration because you already passed the properties, but the component now wants you to use a second method instead 2. It creates confusion, you might be looking at properties when you should be looking at CSS... I think it would be simpler for users to only pass properties.
author: TheThirdRace

body:
Why remove the priority on `raw` layout?

There's  a difference between:
- `raw` as in "no NextJs responsive layout so you have control on the styling"
- `raw` as in "it's a barebone component, you do everything yourself"

The way `raw` was described is the former, not the later.

Thus `raw` should benefit from `priority` as you want to remove NextJs styling, not remove the optimization you'd get from preloading if you pass the prop.

> The reason those props were added is because you used to not be able to use inline style:
> 
> ```js
> <Image src={src} layout="fill" style={{objectFit: "cover"}} />
> ```

I would add it was also added because we can't target the images easily by pure CSS selectors. Which is still a much needed feature one year after the launch of `next/image` :(

I would argue it was also a bit arbitrary that only `objectFit` and `objectPosition` were targeted to be props in this context. A class on each wrapper would have made it super easy to add all the CSS styling you want without resorting to using props, inline styles or DOM bloating. Separation of concerns is a big thing for a lot of people.
author: TheThirdRace

body:
You could use the height/width for setting the aspect ratio so the browser knows what space to reserve to reduce CLS.

The browser will try to optimize before any sizer or padding trick. From my experience, the CLS is still there, but almost zero. The SVG sizer and padding tricks are really only needed to reduce your already low 0.05 CLS to 0...

I'm not 100% sure on this one, but if you keep the height/width, I think the browser will use the calculated aspect ratio and the available space to choose the right version to download from the `srcset`.

What I'm 100% sure, removing the height/width will not benefit you in any way. Furthermore, people using the `raw` layout are most likely gonna want to control their image entirely, which means removing a value they specifically passed is most likely not wanted.

body: I agree with @kara , the whole purpose of `raw` is to not add layout behaviors. The "responsive" behavior from the browser is to download the right image version according to `height`, `width`, `sizes` and `srcset` attributes. Nothing should come in the way of of this. I'd even argue if a user passes `srcset` prop when in `raw` layout, the values from the user should be passed directly to the `` without any modification. I think a default of `1x`/`2x` or `640w, 750w, ...,3840w` depending if `sizes` is set or not is fine, just don't prevent people from generating their own `srcset`. What I consider should always be `640w, ...3840w` might be different for another person and vice versa. The whole point of `raw` is to give back the power to users, defaults are welcome if not forced on you.

body:
What it's doing now, which I think is probably the best compromise, is adding height and width unless you use `sizes`. Sizes should only be used for responsive images, so it doesn't really make sense to include a fixed height and width. Also, having those height and width attributes on a responsive image can mess up a user's intended responsive behavior. For instance, if the user sets a responsive width without realizing that there's a fixed height still attached to the image, it will stretch out the image.

Finally, I'm now adding a `aspect-ratio` style to all raw images. As discussed in the past this still misses a couple of supported browsers, but it should go a long way toward preventing CLS in the responsive case.

TLDR: Images using raw layout with a user-provided responsive styling could (possibly but not likely) suffer from CLS on ie11 and old versions of other browsers. The share of users on such browsers will decrease over time.

body:
I don't think that either`toMatchInlineSnapshot` or `toMatch` would be the right choice here, since the `stderr` string contains a lot of machine specific information such as absolute paths
i.e. 
`at new Input (/Users/baruchadi/projects/next/next.js/packages/next/node_modules/postcss/lib/input.js:24:13)`

and given that the string is about 60 lines long and has more than than 6500 characters (see example value here: https://gist.github.com/baruchadi/81be9d5b4d1f45d6f1f22b2195777a9a), I believe that `.toContain` would be our best bet at the moment. 
We can do `.toMatch` with some regex, but that would require us to make a lot of assumptions and the result would be very similar to `.toContain`.

**Note** that in the code, i'm checking for two new lines before and after our clean message. this should guarantee that the stack was removed from above and below our message.

see the diff between our error message and the original unedited one 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3421731/157109430-caa4eb03-08a3-4077-84e6-7ffb877cabde.png)

body: I think it's actually the opposite: Next.js should be configured with a timeout that is _larger_ than the LB's timeout. See here: https://adamcrowder.net/posts/node-express-api-and-aws-alb-502/ We had 502s and set our timeout slightly higher than the LBs and that resolved them for us.
author: mAAdhaTTah

body:
See also here: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/application-load-balancers.html#connection-idle-timeout

> We also recommend that you configure the idle timeout of your application to be larger than the idle timeout configured for the load balancer. Otherwise, if the application closes the TCP connection to the load balancer ungracefully, the load balancer might send a request to the application before it receives the packet indicating that the connection is closed. If this is the case, the server refuses the request from the load balancer and then the load balancer sends an HTTP 502 Bad Gateway error to the application.

body:
```suggestion
When deploying Next.js behind a downstream proxy (e.g. a load-balancer like AWS ELB/ALB) it's important to configure Next's underlying HTTP server with [keep-alive timeouts](https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#http_server_keepalivetimeout) that are _larger_ than the downstream proxy's timeouts. Otherwise, once a keep-alive timeout is reached for a given TCP connection, Node.js will immediately terminate that connection without notifying the downstream proxy. This results in a proxy error whenever it attempts to reuse a connection that Node.js has already terminated.
```

body:
```suggestion
All SSR pages have the ability to render components into streams and the client continues receiving updates from these streams even after the initial SSR response is sent. When any suspended components resolve down the line, they are rendered on the server and streamed to the client. This means applications can start emitting HTML even _before_ all the data is ready, improving your app's loading performance.

As an added bonus, in streaming SSR mode the client will also use selective hydration to prioritize component hydration based on user interactions, further improving performance.
```

If they use the Node.js runtime, they will have streaming if Next.js is running in a Node.js server. And if it's running in a lambda function that doesn't support streaming, the response will be buffered and sent all at once when everything is ready.

body:
IMHO it is not the correct fix.

The code here is designed to work like this:

- When you specify a custom 404 in `exportPathMap`:
  - Next.js shouldn't overwrite your custom 404 export alias.
- When you don't specify a custom 404 in `exportPathMap` (when, and only when neither `/404` nor `/404.html` exists in `exportPathMap`):
  - When `trailingSlash` is disabled (which is by default):
    - only `404.html` should be exported (which could be used to render `https://example.com/404`).
    - `['/404', '/404.html']` will be deduped to `/404` after path normalization
  - When `trailingSlash` is enabled:
    - should export `404/index.html` instead (which could be used to render `https://example.com/404/`).
    - A `404.html` should also be exported for backward compatibility with GitHub Pages, GitLab Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, etc.
    - So, `/404` would export `/404/index.html` and `/404.html` would export `/404.html`.

You could take a look at `export/worker.ts` to see how it handles the 404 (check the `isBultinPaths` part). Also, an integration test case to verify your fix would be appreciated.

body:
I'd frame this as ordered reading. Even though it is *functionally* not doing this, the behavior is as if the person is checking each place in order, each time and serves as a good mental model.

```suggestion
Environment variables are looked up in the following places, in order, stopping once the variable is found.

1. `process.env`
1. `.env.$(NODE_ENV).local`
1. `.env.local` (Not checked when `NODE_ENV` is `test`.
1. `.env.$(NODE_ENV)`
1. `.env`

For example, if you define a variable in both `.env.local` and `.env`, the value in `.env.local` will be used.
```

#### Match paths based on custom matcher config
To decide which route the middleware should be run on, you can use a custom matcher config to filter on specific paths. The matcher property can be used to define either a single path, or using an array syntax, multiple paths.

##### Match a single path

```js
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*'
}
```

##### Match multiple paths

```js
export const config = {
  matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*']
}
```

body:
````suggestion
## New user agent helper

### Summary of changes

- User agent no longer available on the request object
- New helper introduced
- Reduces Middleware size by 17kB

### Explanation

To help reduce the size of your Middleware, we have extracted the user agent from the request, and created a new helper to interact with the user agent object. 

The helper is imported from `next/server` and allows you to opt in to using the user agent. The helper gives you access to the same properties that were available from the request object.

### How to upgrade

- Import the `userAgent` helper from `next/server`
- Destructure the properties you need to work with

#### Before

```typescript
// middleware.ts
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from 'next/server'

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const url = request.nextUrl
  const viewport = request.ua.device.type === 'mobile' ? 'mobile' : 'desktop'
  url.searchParams.set('viewport', viewport)
  return NextResponse.rewrites(url)
}
```

#### After

```typescript
// middleware.ts
import { NextRequest, NextResponse, userAgent } from 'next/server'

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const url = request.nextUrl
  const { device } = userAgent(request)
  const viewport = device.type === 'mobile' ? 'mobile' : 'desktop'
  url.searchParams.set('viewport', viewport)
  return NextResponse.rewrites(url)
}
```

````

body:
> Thanks! Would you mind explaining why is it more performant? Because it checks `query` before other properties?

It contains serveral optimizations:

- Use `for .. in` on an object will iterate over object's prototype. Use `for .. in` on `Object.keys` fixes that.
- `Route['state'].query` comes from `querystring.parse` where the shape of the parsed query is likely to change. The code checks the shape of the object before checking the value.
- The shape of `Route['state']` is not likely to change, so it is not necessary to check the shape before value.
- Since `routerState.query` is more likely to change, checking it before other state could return early.
- The implementation also caches / re-use the result of `Object.keys` (and its length) to increase the performance even more.

body:
Do not use `useEffect` to sync props to state. React allows updating a state during the render phase (and it behaves just like `getDerivedStateFromProps`).

Before:

- The parent component `<Image />` receives an update, and `useIntersection` receives a new `rootRef`.
- The parent component `<Image />` finishes the update and render.
- The side-effect commit happens **after** the render phase, and the new `rootRef` is synced to state `root`.
- The identity of `setRef` changes (since `setRef` is wrapped inside a `useCallback` with `root` inside the dependencies array).
- Because the identity of `setRef` changes, the parent component `<Image />` has to update again, causing the extra render.

After:

- The parent component `<Image />` receives an update, and `useIntersection` receives a new `rootRef`.
- During `useIntersection` execution, the `root` state updates.
- React immediately exits the current update of `<Image />` components, and starts a new update.
- And the `<Image />` component only renders once.

body:
**Before the PR**

- `setIntersection` is used in `<Image />`'s callback ref, which will be called when `<Image />` is first mounted.
- During `setIntersection`, an IntersectionObserver instance is created and it observes the `HTMLImageElement` with `rootRef.current` is still `null`
- By the time `<Image />` is mounted, its parent element (`lazyRoot`) hasn't been mounted yet, so `lazyRoot` has a value of `{ current: null }`.
- By the time the `setRoot` effect is committed, an IntersectionObserver instance is already created, and the `lazyRoot` is never applied to the IntersectionObserver instance

**After the PR**

- `setIntersection` is used in `<Image />`'s callback ref, which will be called when `<Image />` is first mounted.
- During `setIntersection`, the `HTMLImageElement` is synced to a ref (use ref instead of state to prevent extra re-rendering)
- By the time `useEffect` commits the effect, `lazyRoot` is already mounted, and the `elementRef.current` also exists (it is set during `<Image />` mounting)
- Only then (during the effect) the observer is created with `lazyRoot` applied.

----

In short: The `IntersectionObserver` is a web API (DOM API) and should be considered as a side-effect. A side-effect shouldn't be executed inside DOM's callback ref.

> Do we still need to store the element reference in a `useState()` since when `setRef` is called we update the reference here but we aren't re-calling the `useEffect` above so we won't observe the new ref unless the parent component re-renders?
>
> Or are we changing this hook to have the assumption that the ref passed to setRef should always only change when the parent re-renders?

Here is what I thought. `setRef` here is only supposed to be called after component mounts. In `<Image />` and `<Link />` case, it is called inside the [callback ref](https://reactjs.org/docs/refs-and-the-dom.html#callback-refs).

And the assumption here is that the DOM node itself would remain the same after the component mounts and before unmounts.

body:
> How about `globalThis._testRenderCount` so that its global and doesnt live inside a component and therefor outside of React's jurisdiction

`globalThis._testRenderCount` does live outside of React, but **the modification of this variable has to live inside the `next/image` component** (and probably has to be inside a `useEffect`), which is what I am really concerned about.

As I said before, when a component re-renders, **its parent components will not** always re-render, thus we can't add the `globalThis._testRenderCount` modification in `<Image />`'s parent component (it can't reflect how many times the child component has been updated).

body:
TypeScript is great, but not everyone is writing TypeScript. IMHO we should not use TypeScript to replace the description of each property.

```suggestion
- `isBot`: Whether the request comes from a known bot.
- `browser`
  - `name`: The name of the browser, could be `undefined`.
  - version: The version of the browser, determined dynamically, could be `undefined`.
- `device`
  - `model`: The model of the device, determined dynamically, could be `undefined`.
  - `type`: The type of the browser, can be one of the following values: `console`, `mobile`, `tablet`, `smarttv`, `wearable`, `embedded`, could be `undefined`.
  - `vendor`: The vendor of the device, determined dynamically, could be `undefined`.
- engine
  - name: The name of the browser engine, could be one of the following values: `Amaya`, `Blink`, `EdgeHTML`, `Flow`, `Gecko`, `Goanna`, `iCab`, `KHTML`, `Links`, `Lynx`, `NetFront`, `NetSurf`, `Presto`, `Tasman`, `Trident`, `w3m`, `WebKit`. Could also be `undefined`.
  - version: The version of the browser engine, determined dynamically, could be `undefined`.
- os
  - name: The name of the OS, could be `undefined`.
  - version: The version of the OS, determined dynamically, could be `undefined`.
- cpu
  - architecture: The architecture of the CPU, could be one of the following values: `68k`, `amd64`, `arm`, `arm64`, `armhf`, `avr`, `ia32`, `ia64`, `irix`, `irix64`, `mips`, `mips64`, `pa-risc`, `ppc`, `sparc`, `sparc64`. Could also be `undefined`.
```

Or we could mention that the `userAgent` is built on top of the `ua-parser-js` library and refer to its documentation.

body: Is it expected that a `next/script` `beforeInteractive` tag defined in the body would be moved the `head` automatically? This may confuse users that do want it to be loaded in the body unless we warn for this case or keep it in place.
author: ijjk

body:
Yeah the idea behind `beforeInteractive` is that it should be used sparingly to load a script before any other script on the page (including Next.js chunks). That was always the behavior before we begin enforcing users to place it in `_document.js`, regardless of which component/page it was placed in. I worry that we'll change its intrinsic behavior if we begin to inject scripts in `body` if the user starts placing things there.

However, I understand that it can be confusing for users to place a script in `body` but not see it outputted that way in the DOM. Should I add a console and/or ESLint warning for this? (e.g. "`beforeInteractive scripts will always be inserted into the document head. If you would like to inject a script into the body instead, do this instead...`")

CC @janicklas-ralph for his thoughts too.
author: housseindjirdeh

body:
```suggestion
Middleware runs _before_ cached content, so you can personalize static files and pages. Common examples of Middleware would be authentication, A/B testing, localized pages, bot protection, and more.

The order middleware is applied is:

1. headers from `next.config.js`
2. redirects from `next.config.js`
3. middleware (rewrites, redirects, etc)
4. `beforeFiles` rewrites from `next.config.js`
5. filesystem routes (public/, _next/static/, static pages, etc)
6. `afterFiles` rewrites from `next.config.js`
7. dynamic routes (`/blog/[slug]`)
8. `fallback` rewrites from `next.config.js`
```
We should be sure to document the order middleware is applied in conjunction with custom routes in `next.config.js`

x-ref: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/37797#issuecomment-1166311206

```suggestion
Next.js' default runtime configuration is good for most use cases, but there’re still many reasons to change to one runtime over the other one. ```suggestion
```
```suggestion
To respect the differences in client-side and server-side navigation, and to help ensure that developers do not build insecure Middleware, we are removing the ability to send response bodies in Middleware. This ensures that Middleware is only used to `rewrite`, `redirect`, or modify the incoming request (e.g. [setting cookies](#cookies-api-revamped)).
```

author: ethomson

body:
```suggestion
- **Faster execution with lower latency**: With nested Middleware, a single request could invoke multiple Middleware functions. A single Middleware means a single function execution, which is more efficient.
- **Less expensive**: Middleware usage is billed per invocation. Using nested Middleware, a single request could invoke multiple Middleware functions, meaning multiple Middleware charges per request. A single Middleware means a single invocation per request and is more cost effective.
- **Middleware can conveniently filter on things besides routes**: With nested Middleware, the Middleware files were located in the `pages` directory and Middleware was executed based on request paths. By moving to a single root Middleware, you can still execute code based on request paths, but you can now more conveniently execute Middleware based on other conditions, like `cookies` or the presence of a request header.
- **Deterministic execution ordering**: With nested Middleware, a single request could match multiple Middleware functions. For example, a request to `/dashboard/users/*` would invoke Middleware defined in both `/dashboard/users/_middleware.ts` and `/dashboard/_middleware.js`. However, the execution order is not easy to reason about. Moving to a single, root Middleware more explicitly defines execution order.
- **Supports Next.js Layouts (RFC)**: Moving to a single, root mMddleware helps support the new [Layouts (RFC) in Next.js](https://nextjs.org/blog/layouts-rfc).
```

body:
Hey Brandon, Thanks for opening the issue, I know it's important to Blitz.

I left a comment re: using webpack plugins to expose this config but I also want to provide some commentary on what we are considering for Errors in general.

We aren't yet sure what the right API is for the error handling interface that next should expose because it may end up layering other capabilities on top of what React already provides with transporting server errors to the client. I would be somewhat surprised if we just exposed the onRecoverableError callback as is because there are many things it does not cover. For instance often when there is a server Error there is a preceding `console.error` with a more specific message that is the right clue for debugging the cause of some issue. When these occur on the server today they stay there because React does not forward them the way it does for thrown Errors.

We have not yet started our project to revamp error handling because a few other priorities have come up but we should begin to look at it in the coming weeks when some other projects land.
author: gnoff

body: We should expose a means to configure an error handler in code rather than configuration so that code tooling can operate on it and to avoid potential issues of serializing functions. That said I'm going to leave some broader context on what we are thinking re: errors and I don't have specific guidance on what the api should look like just yet

body:
> And one doubt, `.hydrateRoot` called only once nah?

The original code works like this:

- Is variable `reactRoot` defined as a `ReactDOMClient.Root`?
  - No, `reactRoot` is null: Call `ReactDOMClient.hydrateRoot` to initiate it.
  - Yes, `reactRoot` is not null: Simply call `ReactDOMClient.Root.render` to update the existing React nodes.

That's why there is an `if (!reactRoot)` and a `reactRoot.render` in `client/app-index.tsx`. It is to make sure that no matter how many times `reactRenderElements` itself is being called, the method is still bullet-proof and no race condition.

But now you just break it. `Returntype<typeof requestIdleCallback>` is `number`, not `ReactDOMClient.Root`.

So let's say, `reactRenderElements` itself is being called twice.

- First time `reactRenderElements` is being called, `reactRoot` is `null`.
- `reactRoot = requestIdleCallback(() => { /** */ })`, now `reactRoot` is a `number`.
- The second time `reactRenderElements` is being called, `reactRoot` is not `null`
- `reactRenderElements` will execute `reactRoot.render`
- Now it throws an error: `Uncaught TypeError: <number>.render is not a function`

body:
I've tried various things, and discussed it with the edge team.

We believe the current behavior is right: attempt to access a property, function or constructor of an imported node.js module should throw.

Returning an empty object would confuse users because the thrown error is too generic:
```js
import os from 'os'
os.homedir === undefined
os.homedir() // throws TypeError "os.homedir is not a function"
```
Knowing whether "it's not actually leveraged" can not be done at runtime with an empty object. It requires static parsing and instrumentation, which prove to be unreliable in the past, and lead to this PR to change the behavior.

Now, the good news for Vercel Front is that, by simply bumping `@microlink/mql` to the latest and keep using its lightweight version, it won't use clean-stack and the error will be gone! CC @Kikobeats.

So, there's one specific case that's the problem, where the user uses the `fill` mode on the image, but does not include height or width styling on the container element. In this case, the container element takes the intrinsic size of the image, even though `object-fit: "contain"` is set. This will cause layout shift.

This doesn't happen if the `img` element has `position: "absolute"` and the container element has `position: "relative"`. I haven't found any other techniques for keeping the unsized container from taking the size of the image.

My take is that if someone is adding `height` and `width` to an image in `fill` mode, 90%+ of the time it's going to be because they are making an error--they think that it will do something, and they're going to be confused about why it isn't having any effect.

body:
Yeah, it's going to be very easy to break the fill mode no-layout-shift guarantee by targeting the image with CSS, and I don't think there's anything we can really do about it. We COULD do a runtime check on the image's computed CSS position attribute, but I'm not sure we want to do that, as there are some cases where the image doesn't need position:absolute (such as if the containing element has an assigned height and width) so it wouldn't technically be wrong to change it.

I'm kind of on the fence about whether we should keep this check here, since it is one place where we have visibility into how the user is applying styles to the image, and we could at least warn them off from making certain basic mistakes.

body:
IMHO, adding `memo` to those components is unnecessary. Instead, you should consider `next/*` components as the fundamental building blocks of any Next.js project.

For instance, the `next/image` component can be used in `<Avatar />`, in `<Posts />`, in wherever you want. Thus the `next/image` prop is constantly changing, effectively making the `memo()` completely useless.

As for `next/head`, the component is dependent on its `children` prop (Yes, it is hard for new React developers to realize that the `children` is actually a "render prop"), and every time the parent of `next/head` updates, `next/head` will receive a fresh collection `children` (a collection of newly created JavaScript Object returned by either `React.createElement()` or React new JSX transform `_jsx()`), unless you have wrapped the `children` of `next/head` in `useMemo`. So in most cases, memoing `next/head` is also completely useless.

If you really believe the performance bottleneck of your project is `next/*` components, wrap their parent components (`<Avatar />`, `<Post />`, etc.) in the `memo()` instead. React reconcile will ignore diff for any children of a memoized component.
