body:
```suggestion
First, the value of `sizes` is used by the browser to determine which size of the image to download, from `next/future/image`'s automatically-generated source set. When the browser chooses, it does not yet know the size of the image on the page, so it selects an image that is the same size or larger than the viewport. The `sizes` property allows you to tell the browser that the image will actually be smaller than full screen. If you don't specify a `sizes` value in an image with the `fill` property, a default value of `100vw` (full screen width) is used.
```

body:
Summary of the issue:
1. Hidden iframes are not guaranteed to ever run callbacks schedule through `requestAnimationFrame`. [This table](https://www.vector-logic.com/blog/posts/on-request-animation-frame-and-embedded-iframes#browser_variations) breaks it down browser to browser. For example, on Chrome, `window.requestAnimationFrame` is available, but the callback is never called in a hidden cross-origin iframe.
2. `displayContent` (below) is passed as an option to `beforeRender` which is [specifically `await`-ed](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/0f99768f9811fdf027a083471bd2a435f6207f4a/packages/next/client/index.tsx#L436) before hydrating the app. If `displayContent` never resolves, the app **never** hydrates.

@magic-akari  Is it possible to preserve the original specifier?

E.g.:

```ts
const componentRoot = '@/some-components'
const Component1 = dynamic(() => import(`${componentRoot}/component1`));
const Component2 = dynamic(() => import(`${componentRoot}/component2`));
```

.. should turn into:

```ts
const componentRoot = '@/some-components'
[require.resolveWeak(`${componentRoot}/component1`]
[require.resolveWeak(`${componentRoot}/component2`]
```

It is up to Webpack to handle, evaluate and resolve `require.resolveWeak`, so we could leave the entire `TemplateLiteral` as-is (instead of asserting the `TemplateLiteral` only contains quasis).

body:
IMHO implementing an HTTP cache on Node.js from scratch is really, really, really a bad idea. Too many edge cases to handle (E.g., `cache: 'only-if-cached'` should return `504 Gateway Timeout` when cache missed), too many RFCs and specs to follow, and it is very difficult to truly mimic the browser's cache behavior.

If an HTTP cache is a must-have, use the existing library like [http-cache-semantics](https://www.npmjs.com/package/http-cache-semantics).

> Also notice that the `http-cache-semantics` doesn't support the `Headers` object. You need to transform the `Headers` object into plain object before passing to `http-cache-semantics`

Here is an example: package [make-fetch-happen](https://github.com/npm/make-fetch-happen), made and used by npm, which adds cache support to fetch (built on top of `http-cache-semantics`).
And another example: package [@adobe/helix-fetch](https://github.com/adobe/helix-fetch), which also implements cache support (which is also built on top of `http-cache-semantics`).

body:
Per React documents:

> `React.startTransition` lets you mark updates inside the provided callback as transitions.

However, calling `loadScript` will not trigger an "update" (`loadScript` will not cause a state update or trigger a re-render, as it manipulates DOM directly, bypassing React completely). 

Besides, currently `next/script` component is not concurrent rendering safe at all (see #40025), and calling concurrent API will cause the component (and its children) to opt-in concurrent rendering. If you add `startTransition` inside `next/script`, you may trigger many hidden race conditions.

body:
This is going to lead to more headaches than expected. CSS allows `\` to escape unicode chars without a `u` prefix, eg `"\2022"` should render a `•`, and `"\0025a0"` should render a `■`. Both of these are illegal escape sequences (they're legacy octal escapes in JS), but perfectly fine in CSS.

Rather than use JS's cooking semantics, we can manually cook the raw strings using CSS semantics. We can pilfer SWC's escape parser to do this: https://github.com/swc-project/swc/blob/decebadff1686adb8ea30d0ef84d849061205c7c/crates/swc_css_parser/src/lexer/mod.rs#L892-L969

According to the WICG Priority Hints draft:

> With in-viewport images, a browser may automatically detect if the image is important and boost priority if it gets to layout early enough.

As the draft described, the browser could have detected the in-view image and automatically boost the fetch priority, it is probably unnecessary to dynamically set the `fetchpriority`.

Instead of dynamically setting `fetchpriority` to `high` when intersected and removing the `fetchpriority` when out of the viewport, personally I'd prefer setting a static `fetchpriority`.

`next/image` component already accepts the `priority={boolean}` prop. Would you like to change the implementation so that the `fetchpriority="high"` is set when `priority={true}` is specified?

Query string values should likely take precedence over params.

I think the original RFC was hinting at that `query` was supposed to be the query string (URL search params) only, anyway: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/9524#:~:text=query%20%2D%20The%20query%20string%20(not%20entirely%20sure%20about%20this%20one%2C%20but%20probably%20needed)

Our docs says that `query` is:
> An object representing the query string, including dynamic route parameters.

But does not clarify if the query string value would be prioritized over the dynamic param value if they have the same key (ie. given `[id].js` and `/foo?id=bar`, should `query` resolve to `{id: "bar"}` instead of `{id: "foo"}`)? IMO it should. To get the dynamic param values, there is already `params`.

https://nextjs.org/docs/api-reference/data-fetching/get-server-side-props#context-parameter

```suggestion
> **Note:** If you are incrementally migrating to a dynamic route (e.g. `[slug].js`) and using `fallback` for your `rewrites`, ensure you consider the case where pages are not found. By default, Next.js will match the dynamic route and end the routing phase. Using `notFound: true` in `getStaticProps` would return the `404.js` page content, or the default 404 page. If this is not desired, you can use `getServerSideProps` with `stale-while-revalidate` Cache-Control headers instead of `notFound: true`. Then, you can _manually_ proxy your existing backend using something like [http-proxy](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/38839#discussioncomment-3744442).
```

I think this could be even better
author: leerob

body:
```suggestion
> **Note:** If you are incrementally migrating to a dynamic route (e.g. `[slug].js`) and using `fallback: true` or `fallback: 'blocking'` along with a fallback `rewrite`, ensure you consider the case where pages are not found. When Next.js matches the dynamic route it stops checking any further routes. Using `notFound: true` in `getStaticProps` will return the 404 page without applying the fallback `rewrite`. If this is not desired, you can use `getServerSideProps` with `stale-while-revalidate` Cache-Control headers when returning your props. Then, you can _manually_ proxy to your existing backend using something like [http-proxy](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/38839#discussioncomment-3744442) instead of returning `notFound: true`.
```

It would be useful but I'm not inclined to support it in this PR because:

- It's not obvious what it does: does it *add* headers to existing ones or does it *replace* all existing headers with the object?
- Ambiguity of headers: what if, for example, the user specify `{ Cookie: 'a=b', cookie: 'c=d' }`?

`Headers` nicely prevents these traps. I think *adding* new headers by specifying an object here is convenient but I'd hear feedbacks to be sure 😄

body:
For `json()`, yes. We don't allow returning a response in Next.js middleware so adding this feature to `json()` is meaningless and confusing.

Secondly, we (web servers) can't specify request headers in redirections (`redirect`) because browsers make another request, while `next()` and `rewrite()` are handled internally in server-side.

body:
The point of this is to inform the user that errors are being ignored.

Currently a user of NextJS has no way of knowing that “Checking validity of types” does not check the validity of all types. It’s surprising to the user,  when running `tsc`, to find it produces different results than `next build`.

For example, NextJS currently warns when it modifies the users tsconfig, but not when it changes the results or exit code. This is unexpected.

Solutions can come in many forms
- Updating documentation (best paired with an option below)
- Updating existing “Checking validity of types” logs
- Add a warning (what I chose)
- Stop ignoring type errors


The idea is that through a change like one of the above, developers will know that some type errors are being ignored. If you dislike the messaging, perhaps it would be more clear if I mentioned that the user can run tsc for more information, or we could print the test file diagnostics as a warning as well.

Did that clarify things?

body:
Are we sure we don't want to trigger another pending refresh state if a new update came in while we were updating? A new update might clear up the errors that happened _during_ the previous update. Furthermore, in the exit condition, `onBuildOk` will be called **twice** instead of just once, since we will also call in the `else` branch below. I believe this logic is incorrect and we should do the following instead:

```suggestion
      tryApplyUpdates(
        onBeforeHotUpdate,
        onHotUpdateSuccess
      )
```

In which case we no longer need to pass these two functions as arguments to `tryApplyUpdates`, we can inline them directly instead.

I looked into getting rid of it, but unfortunately [`URLSearchParams` doesn't support nested objects](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLSearchParams/URLSearchParams#parameters), so I believe in this case `qs` is necessary.

`react-instantsearch` passes nested objects and arrays, which `URLSearchParams` can't convert. So we can't easily stringify/parse nested data structures without `qs` or some [Leetcode Hard-style solution](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56173848/want-to-convert-a-nested-object-to-query-parameter-for-attaching-to-url#answer-65831379).

body:
I'm not sure if this is an intended or unintended consequence, but this causes issues with CDNs that are configured to cache the routes `https://nextjs.org/_next/data/...`

With this change, the server would return an empty body `{}` for requests with the `x-middleware-prefetch` header which may be incidentally cached by the CDN.

For CDNs that do not allow configuring cache keys by custom headers such as Cloudflare, this empty body will be cached.

And if the user will then try to navigate to the "prefetched page", the Next.js application will throw an exception because it is then trying to load the same `https://nextjs.org/_next/data/...` URL without the `x-middleware-prefetch` header expecting the server-side props to be returned, but instead gets back `{}`.

body:
Synchronous != Fast. Synchronous means that if you do more than one thing, you do it more than once. For example, in this case cause reflows more than once. So synchronous means slower. (Same thing in React. Transitions can be faster than synchronous.)

IntersectionObserver should fire before the next rAF so it should be async but before painting. If that's not happening it might be because the React render itself is too late but that since odd since React itself doesn't render a transition during these events. So seems like something is off.

Previously, this section had 2 sections:

However, this organization was a bit confusing. Regular expressions should be less frequently used than case helpers, but it was explained *before* case helpers. The regex section was using syntaxes like `matches.[1]` before it was explained in the handlebars templating section.

So I reversed the order of explanations. Furthermore, I combined them into 1 section as "Handlebars variables and helper functions", as the handlebars templating section had a brief explanation of regexes, so it made more sense to keep them together.

What would this change do in terms of my expectations in my tests? As they seem fine and I want to make sure I cover all the cases (kind of a TDD approach) because stack traces are tricky Seems that using async/await is necessary in any way to track the stack correctly. Floating promises and/or returning a `Promise` without awaiting seem to break stack traces no matter what. body:
I don't know how to run the test suite, so I'm making assumptions:

> Seems that using async/await is necessary in any way to track the stack correctly. Floating promises and/or returning a `Promise` without awaiting seem to break stack traces no matter what.

This is the core problem, and I think it's why your tests are passing. You're using `await`s all the way down your chain, which the user is not always guaranteed to do. If the user has any promise usage, then we've lost the context from before that promise.

To illustrate this, I've made https://github.com/jridgewell/stack-trace-async-event, where "current" is the current production behavior, "PR" is this PR's behavior, and "Final" is the behavior I'm trying to propose. With this PR, we're broken in promise code, and fixed in await code.

The cases that match this PR are 4, 5, 6. The difference between them is how whether we `await` the promise in the current function. If the user only uses `await`, and does it for the entire call stack, we're fine (and that's what's tested). But if a user uses a Promise in the stack, then that promise frame will be ommitted (case 5). And if the user only uses promise, then all frames are omitted (case 4).

With my proposed `source` error stack capturing, we fix this. It won't matter if the user used promises or await, because we won't depend on V8's async stack stitching (which only works for `await`). Instead, we'll have access to the stack at the moment the `fetch` was called (lazily, too, via the `source` error's stack). That will capture the async and sync calls stack that got us to this point, which will include promises.



> But if there's an edge case I don't cover, I'd like to add it to the tests so it will be explicitly tested and your suggestion would be the fix

For test cases, we need to throw in some non-awaited promises. See https://github.com/jridgewell/stack-trace-async-event/blob/main/7-promises-capture-source.js and https://github.com/jridgewell/stack-trace-async-event/blob/main/8-some-async-awaits-capture-source.js to complement you're already existing https://github.com/jridgewell/stack-trace-async-event/blob/main/9-all-async-awaits-capture-source.js.

body:
Start and stop profiler could be costly.

Even when assuming the profiler itself has 0 overhead, adding an `await` means the server has to wait for an extra microtask before serving a response (According to the ES Spec, the engine should always queue a microtask when a promise is being `await`-ed, even if that promise has already been resolved).
author: SukkaW

body:
Having a branch (`if (!PROFILER_ENABLED)`) for every incoming request could be slow (It is a hot path. If the engine is having trouble optimizing this, this would be a performance overhead).

The creator of [Bluebird](https://github.com/petkaantonov/bluebird/) (Bluebird is one of the fastest JavaScript Promise implementations to this day, even comparable to the V8 native) has introduced an approach in [his blog post *Three JavaScript performance fundamentals that make Bluebird fast*](https://www.reaktor.com/blog/javascript-performance-fundamentals-make-bluebird-fast/) called "Use no-op functions and overwrite them lazily to implement costly optional features", here I quote:

> Checking if the monitoring feature is enabled before making the call to the hook function would be better than just making the call regardless of if the feature is enabled. However, the cost can actually be completely eliminated for users that have not enabled the feature thanks to inline caches and function inlining. This can be done by making the initial hook method just an empty function.
>
> Now, if the user doesn’t enable the monitoring feature, the optimizer sees that the function call doesn’t do anything and eliminates it. So the call to the hook method inside the constructor effectively doesn’t exist.
>
> To make the feature actually work, the act of enabling the feature must overwrite all the related no-op functions with the actual implementations.
author: SukkaW

body:
Yet another case where `as any` is a Bad 😈 

Explaining: `createContext` is a hard API to get type safe. Its typings indicate that you must provide a default value for it: that way, when it's called, it's known to always return a value. (In more technical terms, `createContext<T>` takes in a parameter of type `T` so the return type is `T`, not `T | undefined`.)

Unfortunately that means that when there isn't a reasonable default value -the majority of the time in my experience 🙃- projects tend to provide something bogus like `null as any` to get around type checking. They then assume `useContext` will only be called with that context in places where someone has used that context's provider to provide a real value.

The assumption that someone's provided an overridden value isn't always correct! We see in this PR's linked bug #45024 that if someone renders `<Html>` outside of `pages/_document.(js|tsx)`, Next.js hasn't provided a context value with `HtmlContext.Provider`. So when code tries `const { ... } = useContext(HtmlContext)`, that evaluates to `const { ... } = undefined`, which is a runtime error. 

This PR doesn't change whether an error is thrown. It just throws a nicer error for users to read.

body:
Per Next.js documentation: https://nextjs.org/docs/basic-features/supported-browsers-features

Next.js only includes polyfills to support up to **ES2019**. Currently, no further polyfill should be added in the `next-polyfill-module` as it will result in a client-side bundle size increase.

Since `globalThis` is introduced in **ES2020** which is not prior to ES2019, Next.js should not include this polyfill by default.

If you want to introduce the polyfill for ES2020 features (like `globalThis`), then you should also polyfill every ES2020 feature in order to maintain behavior consistency (to prevent future issues like "why globalThis is polyfilled but `String.prototype.matchAll` is not"):

- globalThis
- ~~BigInt~~ - it is not polyfill-able
- Promise.allSettled()
- String.prorotype.matchAll

See also: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/eslint-plugin-next/src/rules/no-unwanted-polyfillio.ts

body:
As it stands, the router will only strip the base path off of some routes, but not all (see thread https://vercel.slack.com/archives/C04KC8A53T7/p1675873382812609). We have two options:
1. Have the JS router strip the base path off of every route, even those it doesn't know about; or
2. Have the JS router ignore the base path entirely, leaving it to Turbopack to handle, and only return results for rewrites/redirects.

On Turbopack's side, the second option would be best as we already need to be aware of the base path anyway.

body:
one semantic thing that go lost in recent refactors but is probably a mistake.

Page metadata is not at a lower layer than Layout metadata. This is important when considering which title template applies.

```
/app/layout.js -> template "%s - root"
/app/deep/layout.js -> template "%s - deep"
/app/deep/page.js -> title "page"
```
we want to see the rendered title for /deep/page as `"page - root"` not `"page - deep"`.

I believe the way things currently stand we would end up with `page - deep`. This might require having both Layout and Page metadata on the same metadataItem instance. The nice thing is that it will always be the last item b/c there are no items deeper than Page so we can do our special logic once our iterator hits the last pass through

body:
Is it correct that `metadataItems` only has entries if the layout or page exports `metadata` or `generateMetadata`?

I believe that is the case which is why I think the earlier approach of tracking whether the Layout was a leaf layout or not is actually right approach.

We need to know if `metadataItems[metadataItems.length - 1]` is a Page
We need to know if `metadataItems[metadataItems.length - 2]` is a Layout at the same level as `metadataItems[metadataItems.length - 1]`

isLeafLayout (if calculated correctly) tells us exactly this
If it isLeafLayout and there are no more metadataItems then there is nothing special to do
If it isLeaflayout and there is one more metadataItem then it must be the Page at the same level
If it is not isLeafLayout and there is one more metadataItem then it is a Layout but at a higher up folder level and there is nothing special to do.

I would go back to the old way of handling titles, it is much easier to follow. The only change that we need is to accurately compute isLeafLayout and to slightly modify how we derive the templates to pass to `merge` handling this one special case of leafLayout

body:
The example I mentioned here

> it reduces the possibility of "ESM dependencies that can't be bundled" when a package has both ESM and CJS exports.
> https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/42741#issuecomment-1310601523

is the small case that we **can't** work around at all for precompiled React: if an **ESM** package X can't be bundled (e.g. it uses `__dirname` or something else) and user have to put it inside `serverComponentsExternalPackages`, and it happens to use React inside, we can't map that React to our precompiled one.

That's because the require hook doesn't work for ESM, and our bundling is skipped.

To make it less possible to happen, if X has both ESM and CJS builds (which many packages do), we should prefer CJS in this case. With CJS even if we can't bundle it, the require hook still takes effect here.

body:
This fix breaks the case where there is a route like:

```
app/[locale]/post/[slug]/page.js
```

Where locale management is done in app directory. The underlying issue is because the default locale is injected into paths higher up:

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/9ad1f321b7902542acd2be041fb2f15f023a0ed9/packages/next/src/server/base-server.ts#L687-L689

So the fix would require this beheviour to be stripped out. Instead we should rely on a tweak to the locale detection. Today in the router, we assume the default locale correctly via the `inferDefaultLocale` option:

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/9ad1f321b7902542acd2be041fb2f15f023a0ed9/packages/next/src/server/router.ts#L185-L195

This leaves the underlying `pathname` unchanged but detects the correct locale for the matchers. The incomming request pathname should always include the cleaned pathname (which still includes locale information).

more info on this from @ijjk:

We have a site that generates 208,630 pages, and we've set the env var  `--max_old_space_size=12288` on the main call to `next build` because its running on a kubernetes pod limited to 16GB memory (we need some overhead for the parent process).

We just upgraded to `v13.2.4` which includes this PR, we wanted to see what effect this release had on memory usage, and now we're seeing a _slightly_ different but interesting behavior in the workers: 

```
// snipped of next build output
info  - Compiled successfully
info  - Collecting page data...
Static worker unexpectedly exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL
Static worker unexpectedly exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL
Static worker unexpectedly exited with code: null and signal: SIGTERM
warn  - Restarted collecting page data for [object Object] because it took more than 600 seconds
warn  - See more info here https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/static-page-generation-timeout
warn  - Restarted collecting page data for [object Object] because it took more than 600 seconds
info  - Generating static pages (0/208630)
Static worker unexpectedly exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL
Static worker unexpectedly exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL
Static worker unexpectedly exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL
info  - Generating static pages (732/208630)
info  - Generating static pages (3750/208630)
// snipped
info  - Generating static pages (208630/208630)
info  - Finalizing page optimization...
success
```
but despite these errors the build ended up completing successfully.

Are edge functions multiplexed? The invocation here has some bugs around concurrent use of the ALS:
1. previous value isn't restored

body:
`srcset` is used so devices with smaller screens can download a smaller version of an image - which has a smaller size and will take less time to be downloaded. Image optimizer doesn't upscale source images, so the highest possible resolution is going to be the same as the resolution of the source image. If we would ask it to create versions 1000x1000, 2000x2000, 3000x3000... for an image that has smaller dimensions than that, those versions would be stored in the cache, but actually, all of them will have the same size as the original image.

I will create a test for it and fix failing tests some day during this week.

body:
Mostly implementation detail from early days that I should get rid of soon. It's for manipulating the shape of arguments based on if it's a transpiled action (inlined) or not (file-level).

In a "use server" file we can't transpile all the action functions as we don't know which function will be exported (it's a runtime thing). What we are doing is to wrap all exported fields. Because of that, we don't manipulate the action's argument list during compilation so if a function takes arguments, say `async function action(a, b, c)`, we need to pass these arguments in that shape when invoking the action.

But for inlined actions, since we have an array of bound values + arguments received, a short path (the initial commit of the transpiler) we were taking is to compile the action to `async function action(closure, closure_value_1 = closure[0], a = closure[1], b = closure[2], c = closure[3])` and then calling the action with `action($$bound)`. 

This needs to be fixed as `async function action(closure_value_1, a, b, c)` to make it unified.

body:
The test for middleware rewrite with headers doesn\'t actually verify that the custom header was forwarded to the external API\. It only checks the response status and body\, which would pass even if headers were being dropped entirely\.
View Details
📝 Patch Details ```diff diff --git a/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/app/middleware.js b/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/app/middleware.js index 0a5c72ed62..398dad0129 100644 --- a/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/app/middleware.js +++ b/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/app/middleware.js @@ -29,7 +29,7 @@ export async function middleware(request) { tmpHeaders.set('x-hello-from-middleware1', 'hello') return NextResponse.rewrite( - 'https://next-data-api-endpoint.vercel.app/api/echo-body', + 'https://next-data-api-endpoint.vercel.app/api/echo-headers', { request: { headers: tmpHeaders, diff --git a/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/test/index.test.ts b/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/test/index.test.ts index 237329e852..59ca7f29ad 100644 --- a/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/test/index.test.ts +++ b/test/e2e/middleware-rewrites/test/index.test.ts @@ -84,7 +84,8 @@ describe('Middleware Rewrite', () => { ) expect(res.status).toBe(200) - expect(await res.text()).toEqual(body) + const responseData = JSON.parse(await res.text()) + expect(responseData.headers['x-hello-from-middleware1']).toBe('hello') }) it('should handle static dynamic rewrite from middleware correctly', async () => { ```
### Analysis ## Test for middleware rewrite with headers doesn\'t validate header forwarding **What fails\:** The test `should handle middleware rewrite with body and headers correctly` \(test\/e2e\/middleware\-rewrites\/test\/index\.test\.ts\, lines 75\-88\) only verifies response status and body\, without checking if the custom header `x-hello-from-middleware1: hello` \(set in middleware\.js line 29\) was actually forwarded to the external API endpoint\. **How to reproduce\:** The test calls `/middleware-external-rewrite-body-headers`\, which triggers middleware that\: 1. Sets custom header\: `x-hello-from-middleware1: hello` 2. Rewrites to external API\: `https://next-data-api-endpoint.vercel.app/api/echo-body` The test then validates\: * Response status is 200 * Response body equals the input body But it never validates whether the custom header was forwarded\. **Result\:** Test passes regardless of whether headers are actually forwarded to the external endpoint\. The test would pass even if the middleware header forwarding feature was broken\. **Expected\:** The test should validate that custom headers set in middleware are properly forwarded to the external rewrite destination\. **Fix implemented\:** 1. Changed middleware to rewrite to `/api/echo-headers` \(which returns request headers in the response JSON\) 2. Updated test to parse the JSON response and verify `responseData.headers['x-hello-from-middleware1']` equals `'hello'` This ensures the test actually validates that header modifications in middleware are preserved through the external rewrite process\.
author: vercel

body:
The test now validates that custom headers set in middleware are properly forwarded to the external rewrite destination by calling an endpoint that echoes headers back and asserting that `json.headers['x-hello-from-middleware1']` equals `'hello'`.

body:
This comes back to the discussion around differentiating paths and path types. While both of these file systems map to the same underlying FS and directory, they represent different things. For instance, it doesn't make sense to `.get_path_to()` between a client path and a node path. Any operation that takes two paths of different types should fail or return an empty result.,

This is a way to ensure some basic level of safety when handling paths of different types. I think these should eventually become different types entirely, but for now this is good enough.

body:
`import` is different because it's not a condition of the environment (am I running in a browser? edge? regular node?) but of the way the code is written (do I use `import` syntax or `require()` calls?). If removing `import` leads to unexpected results, then your code is using `require()` calls.

You shouldn't override this, because the imported code could be written in a way designed for CJS or ESM semantics. Eg, I usually `module.exports = something` for CJS, but use `export default something` for ESM. These have different meanings at the importing site, and so the user's code can break if the correct one isn't returned. (Getting the ESM code when using `require()` will mean the user has to `require().default`, and getting CJS code when using `import` syntax will mean the user can't use named imports).

So my biggest question is with the stylesheet stuff. Float opens up a lot of possibilities to optimize the loading but it would make third-party scripts only usable in App Router. Someday when Pages can use React 18.3 or whatever version ships with float we could make it available universally.

If we want this to be Page and App Router compatible from beginning then we're stuck with the current approach but this means we can't SSR the stylesheets and we can't load them ahead of time.

body: Is there a reason to not load the stylesheet earlier than when the script loads? I would imagine any script related stylesheets would not be using global style rules that affect the document except for what the script itself injects/modifies. Seems like loading here is too late and may potentially race between script execution and style application. It'd probably be better to just render these stylesheets wtih the Script component using the precedence prop to opt into Float hoisting. The only problem with this strategy is that it would only work in App Router at the moment.

body:
Something feels a little off to me. I'm new to the implementation of next/script so this is really the first time I've dug in but it seems like you can externally initialize the script state via `handleClientScriptLoad` and `initScriptLoader` which accept prop.

The problem is these props are not augmented the same way the props that are fed to `loadScript` are and you may end up with manually inserted stylesheets if using those methods when a regular render would end up with the rendered stylesheets.

Perhaps instead of rendering the stylesheet with a precedence you use the `ReactDOM.preinit(href, { as: 'style' })` form.

This can be called from loadScript or earlier if we want within the render of the `Script` element. Either way it will ensure that we only load the stylesheet once and in a consistent manner regardless of which pathway the load comes from

Next.js promotes a hybrid approach that allows you to use a combination of [server-side rendering](/docs/pages/building-your-application/rendering/server-side-rendering), [static site generation](/docs/pages/building-your-application/rendering/static-site-generation), and client-side rendering, **depending on the needs of each page** in your application. In the App Router, you can also use [Loading UI with Suspense](/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/loading-ui-and-streaming) to show a loading indicator while the page is being rendered.

body: The tricky thing about this being a linter rule is that, even if a file doesn't have `"use client"` on top, it can still be a Client Component (e.g. it can be imported by a file with `"use client"`). And also, a file with `"use client"` can still export non-component functions that are async. Not strongly against adding such a linter rule, but we can probably make it a warning instead of an error, and ensure that the exported function's name start with a capitalized character.

Thanks for the update! But I would like to clarify something more.

Please imagine that user A and B are viewing the same page at the same time. If user A invokes Server Actions and it calls `revalidatePath`/`Tag`, it will invalidate the Data cache, the Render cache, and the only user A's Router cache.

However, user B's Router cache would not be invalidated, so if the page was statically rendered and prefetched, it would not be up-to-date for 5 minutes. This may seem obvious, but I don't think this is well understood by developers using App Router at this time.

body:
Ok so for me there was quite a big visual difference between 1px and 20px blur placeholder images (1px blur images seemed to be too blurry). I started digging in to find out why and I've found this part right here

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/946c9c5c46091604b8a9c73260bfe26ece70de23/packages/next/src/build/webpack/loaders/next-image-loader/blur.ts#L4
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/946c9c5c46091604b8a9c73260bfe26ece70de23/packages/next/src/build/webpack/loaders/next-image-loader/blur.ts#L42-L54

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/e17218fcba36ef148797dfefd5147e01cb29843b/packages/next/src/shared/lib/get-img-props.ts#L355-L356

So it looks like the "1px" blur is only used for blur placeholders generated by Next.js for staticly imported images (please correct me if I am wrong here) and they're at most 8px wide .

How I tried to figure out a better blur value for these small placeholders (8px wide/high maximum) is by doing simple calculations.

Taking two example images, one 390px wide (an iPhone 12 PRO screen width) and the second one 1512px wide (14" laptop screen width) I calculated the blur ratio bounds assuming the default blur is 20px.

20/1512 = 0.013 ----> 20/390 = 0.05 

Now translating that to 8px wide images:

0.013 * 8 = 0.1 ----> 0.05 * 8 = 0.4

Given that most traffic happens on mobile devices I've decided to go for the upper bound (images of smart phone screen width) and round it to 0.5 (because I know that SVG filters handle decimal halves values well).

## Alternative approach

Switching between different blur values depending on `blurWidth` and `blurHeight` being present seems a bit hacky to me. What we could do instead is to scale the `viewBox` attribute when `blurWidth` and `blurHeight` are set (since we know these values are at most 8px). Instead of doing `viewbox='0 0 8 5'` we could scale it by 50 (to get closer to the normal image size ~ 400px ) and do `viewbox='0 0 400 250'`. This way proportions are kept and blur stays fixed at 20px.

@styfle lmk if my assumptions are correct here and if I have the green light to go this way. 🤓

body:
> This is not accounting for the 3x DPR. You can confirm this by looking in dev tools emulation or by logging window.devicePixelRatio which prints 3.

AFAIK the viewBox doesn't 'care' about the DPI because it just specifies SVG dimensions in user space in px length unit (just like in CSS - width: 1px is actually 2 physical pixels wide for screens of DPI=2):

> The viewBox attribute defines the position and dimension, in user space, of an SVG viewport.

Also if DPI was problematic it would also have to break for the current viewBox/1px blur approach (As it remains constant across all possible DPIs)

> That sounds like it could be a good approach, but where did you get the number 50?

Well I just picked a 400px wide imaginary image for which 20px blur looks perfect. Then calculated the scale value 400px/8px (max blur width) = 50. The scale value of course can be tweaked but from my brief testing round it looked fine. 

Maybe I'll just implement that now, we'll test it and if you approve I'll update all tests so that we're ready to merge?

I think its worth a try because then we'll just have one simple filter that handles all cases no matter where the placeholder blur comes from 🤓

```suggestion
    if (el.tagName === 'SCRIPT' && isBooleanScriptAttribute(attr) && value !== 'false') {
```
Couldn't we avoid setting the initial value here for the `'false'` case and then that should remove the need for the `setAttribute(attr, ''); removeAttribute(attr)` condition below?
author: ijjk

body:
Unfortunately, this will have the same problem that this PR is trying to fix:
- `false`, this will enter this if condition and set the attribute to `false`, which HTML casts to `"false"` which is interpreted as true (non-empty string)
- `"false"`, this will enter the else condition and set the attribute to `"false"` which is interpreted as true (non-empty string)

This also breaks for script elements, which when inserted by JavaScript automatically default to async=true. So for async=false we need to do this setAttribute/removeAttribute trick explicitly. See https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#script-force-async

body:
After I moved `USER` above `COPY` and removed the `--chown` flag, I encountered this error in my production image:

```
Failed to write image to cache +rydQqMXZ0bVZ74cCOHPm9Twi2E8kcPDkF2840NyjL0= [Error: EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/.next/cache'] {
  errno: -13,
  code: 'EACCES',
  syscall: 'mkdir',
  path: '/app/.next/cache'
}
```

Based on Dockerfile docs for `USER` [^1]:

> The USER instruction sets the user name (or UID) and optionally the user group (or GID) to use as the default user and group **for the remainder of the current stage**.

However, based on Dockerfile docs for `COPY` [^2]:

> All new files and directories **are created with a UID and GID of 0**, unless the optional `--chown` flag specifies a given username, groupname, or UID/GID combination to request specific ownership of the copied content.

It appears that the `--chown` is **not redundant** even if we moved `USER` above `COPY`. This matter has been discussed previously in https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/6119.

If we omit `--chown`, the files and directories are owned by `root`. Here is the `ls -al` from my production image:

```
/app $ ls -al
total 52
drwxr-xr-x    1 root     root          4096 Aug 15 06:26 .
drwxr-xr-x    1 root     root          4096 Aug 15 06:35 ..
-rw-r--r--    1 root     root          1879 Aug 15 06:25 .env
drwxr-xr-x    1 root     root          4096 Aug 15 06:26 .next
-rwxr-xr-x    1 root     root            55 Aug 15 06:23 docker-entrypoint.sh
drwxr-xr-x  212 root     root         12288 Aug 15 06:25 node_modules
-rw-r--r--    1 root     root          2517 Aug 15 06:25 package.json
drwxr-xr-x    3 root     root          4096 Aug 15 06:23 prisma
drwxr-xr-x    3 root     root          4096 Aug 15 06:09 public
-rw-r--r--    1 root     root          7891 Aug 15 06:25 server.js
/app $
```

[^1]: https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/#user
[^2]: https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/#copy

body:
We don't bundle the server code all the time yet (I think) and I'm not sure what level of optimization we will end up applying to our bundle when we do. Absent an optimizing step that would inline these function calls it's more performant to just inline the string concatenation.

I realize this is a drop in the bucket compared to overhead in the rest of Next but I think in the long run we're going to want to start caring more about good perf by default and in aggregate little things like this will add up eventually.

There are a couple reasons this would be slower, first a function call itself has overhead. But second the allocation of a new function to create the closure for `assetPrefix` and `qs`. There's obviously a tradeoff (getRequireScripts itself is a function that won't be inlined) but since this repeated string concat is clear in it's intention and self contained I think the repetition is not particularly taxing mental cost and it's not a place we're likely to mistakenly update in a broken way in the future.

I could make a `getSrc(prefix, filename, querystring)` function that is only allocated once for the module but then it's not really saving much character-wise and still adds a function call overhead so I think it's good how it is

body:
### 1s delay downsides with `redirect()` (maybe this should be its own issue/discussion)

Hm, the 1s delay on `redirect()` is not ideal for auth gating ([temporary `redirect()` in either in `page.tsx` or in `layout.tsx`](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Aupleveled%2Fnext-js-example-spring-2023-vienna-austria+redirect%28&type=code)):

- unusual, slow UX (waiting for 1 second)
- switching to `permanentRedirect()` would not be correct semantically (a permanent redirect from a page to `/login` not correct)
- often Middleware is suggested here, but Middleware cannot be used with database auth due to [Middleware lacking support for database TCP connections](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/46722)

Ideally, one of the following seems like more well-rounded solutions without the UX downsides:

A) Middleware TCP support
B) Setting a [`Location` response header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Location) when `redirect()` or `permanentRedirect()` are used - in a style similar to how React Float changes other parts of tree / response

But I guess for now we will consider recommending `permanentRedirect()` to our students for now to avoid the 1s weirdness (tradeoff against the semantically-incorrect "permanent" part)

If a `<meta>` tag is the only thing that can be used for now, I guess the previous solution of 307 + 0s refresh feels at first glance like a better tradeoff... (at least the status code is correct in that case and it doesn't promote a slow UX)
author: karlhorky

body: A simple solution would be to redirect from JavaScript if there is the refresh meta tag so you don’t need to wait the 1 second delay, not sure if the router already does this
author: remorses

body:
The tricky part is around streaming in general. If it's used in a streaming context and HTTP headers are already sent to the client (e.g., with status 200), we can't emit additional headers afterward. This is why meta tag is used this way as far as I understand.

Google warns Javascript redirect to be the last resort to adopt so I guess it's safe to avoid that:
https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects#jslocation

> If it's used in a streaming context and HTTP headers are already sent to the client (e.g., with status 200), we can't emit additional headers afterward

Right, with [my suggestion B above](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/54047#discussion_r1309897346) I meant to "lift up" the `redirect()` / `permanentRedirect()` and logic to an earlier part in the response cycle, so that both the status code and the `Location` header could be set

The moment your components run you can't assume the headers haven't been sent yet. In the near future there will be early hints / preloads that means even before your code runs it's already streaming.

Redirecting for authentication should be handled in middleware if you want it to run in front of any rendering.

body:
We use pages / layouts auth gating as [also recommended as an alternative by Lee](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/46722#:~:text=It%27s%20also%20worth,set%20of%20routes.) - not as a choice, but as a necessity.

We do this because Middleware is not an option. The [Edge Runtime Middleware is not capable of doing auth gating with database auth](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/46722), if you need a TCP connection, which most database options do ([workaround edge database products exist, such as Vercel Postgres / Neon](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/46722#discussioncomment-5790036), but not everyone can use them). So these users of Next.js App Router are currently stuck with pages / layout auth gating.

However, I would love to be able to do this with Middleware, eg. if there will be tangible movement soon about Node.js Runtime Middleware [as mentioned by Lee](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/46722#:~:text=exploring%20ways%20to%20bridge%20the%20gap%20towards%20allowing%20folks%20to%20experimentally/%22dangerously%22%20opt%2Dinto%20using%20the%20Node.js%20Runtime):

body:
Missing a semicolon in IIFE `;(async () => // ...`

I'm assuming that the use of `setTimeout` is intentional so as to create a buffer on the next event loop?
author: devjiwonchoi

body:
The async function is properly encapsulated inside another function, so there's no risk of breakage if some tool inlines this file with other files. And five years ago StackOverflow had this:
>I answered this originally in 2013 and I should point out now that most modern javascript web tools are smart enough to handle this now, and with ES2015 and newer, there's better encapsulation, leading to less IIFEs. I haven't had to use an IIFE in years. – 
[Erty Seidohl](https://stackoverflow.com/users/374601/erty-seidohl)
 [Apr 17, 2018 at 20:03](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/17978883/what-is-the-purpose-of-a-semicolon-before-an-iife#comment86789191_17978926)
 
The buffer requirement is satisfied with the first let statement. flushBuffer is just trying to do its job of flushing the buffer, but setTimeout is the worst way to do this, as the callback is put on the bottom of the stack. SetImmediate would be better, as it goes on the top of the stack, but the anonymous async function is clearly the winner, as the tests show.

Here we have

> `path`: [...] This is [...] not the path on the filesystem `/product/[slug]/page`.

but right below we also have "Revalidating A Page Path" and "Revalidating A Layout Path" sections right below that show code examples of `revalidatePath('/blog/[slug]', ...)`. I think this is a bit confusing. Does `/blog/[slug]` still work? Does the "not the path on the filesystem" sentence mean `/blog/[slug]` does work but `/blog/[slug]/page` doesn't (which is the current behaviour)?
author: joulev

body:
The current described behavior for dynamic routes is a bug, `/blog/[slug]` is only meant to work when the second argument is provided specifying `page` or `layout`. 

By default when only one argument is provided it should be the URL path meant to be revalidated which is what the examples below are trying to show-case and explain.

This will revalidate any URL that matches the provided `page` file on the next page visit. This will _not_ invalidate pages beneath the specific page. For example, `/blog/[slug]` won't invalidate `/blog/[slug]/[author]`.

```suggestion
This will revalidate any URL that matches the provided `layout` file on the next page visit. This will cause pages beneath with the same layout to revalidate on the next visit. For example, in the above case, `/blog/[slug]/[another]` would also revalidate on the next visit.
```

body: This test doesn't make sense to me. If JS is enabled, and the document has hydrated by now, then this will do a normal JS submit. If you want to test the non-JS version, you should either disable JS entirely or do something like throw an infinite promise on the client to block hydration.
author: acdlite

body: Since the `__next_f` stuff is an implementation detail, a better way to test would be to check the value of the `#form-state` element. If it's "initial-state:test" then the progressive enhancement worked correctly.
author: acdlite

body:
I can confirm that when the document has hydrated this still does the browser form submission (not via JS):

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/assets/3676859/71daccda-ccf5-4728-b5c2-ecc293286d98

The non-JS version is tested in the previous test case, this one is for the "non-JS form submission → browser hard navigation → hydration" case. We can't disable JS to test that, because in Playwright we can't re-enable JS on the flight when the navigation starts.

- how do we handle newly added tests? Should they run by default? I would say: run them when the test suite doesn't have failing tests before. So use cases: all when the failing array is empty.
author: sokra

body:
Technically it can't happen that test cases are removed from the list. But this might happen here due to 3 reasons:
- flaky tests
- tests being renamed or removed
- unmerged turbo Updates breaking test cases

I think we should handle them here.

Case 2 can be detected by a test case neither passing nor failing. In this case we can remove it.

Case 1 and 3 looks the same. Test case is failing but was passing before. I think we should keep it in the passing list and print a "potential flaky/broken test" to the console.

Maybe we need to maintain a flaky-tests-manifest.js to disable test cases manually if needed.

body: There were a few situations that I noticed that the pathname data was undefined, so I added some runtime checks. body:
Currently it prioritizes exports in layout, then template and lastly page. Except for if the route does not contain a layout, then it prioritizes page. Once it has found generateStaticParams on a certain route level, it ignores all other exports for that level.

A better solution would be to check if generateStaticParams is exported from multiple files in the same route, and then throw an error. However this requires all these files in the route to be imported (layout, template, page) making for slower build times. Is it worth the trade-off to get good error messages?

I don't think this pattern is edge-case free. When you render this component it will use the initial dataLayer prop to instantiate the script by id. Then afterwards any changes to the dataLayer prop will not be reflected in teh gtm script but will alter this module scoped variable.

The `sendGTMEvent` refers to the current dataLayer rather than the the one initially used instantiate the script so a wayward props update could breat gtm tracking.

If it is true that you can't hot-update the datalayer in GTM (meaning you need to just pick it at the start of the app runtime and never change it) then we should align the module global to only update when the gtm script will actually run which is just once one hte first render.

This is more of a style nit but generally we shouldn't use `instanceof` because 1) it only works on native Promises, not thenable objects 2) it doesn't work cross-realm (i.e. it would fail if the promise came from a worker).

In this case it doesn't matter so much because the promise is owned by Next.js itself but it's good to follow the pattern even in places where it doesn't technically matter so that it doesn't spread to other parts of the codebase.

You can do `typeof actionResult.then === 'function'` instead.

This was to address a scenario where if you fired off a long-running server action, navigations were blocked until the action runs to completion.

I'm also ok with the aborting strategy, but when discussing the first PR that addressed this with @shuding, we decided that it'd be nice if the request ran to completion (and wasn't aborted), even if the result is discarded by the router. 

Here's the test for that scenario: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/test/e2e/app-dir/actions/app-action.test.ts#L271-L289

as well as when it was first reported as a bug (prior to the previous hack that addressed this case): https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/49425
author: ztanner

body:
> I'm also ok with the aborting strategy, but when discussing the first PR that addressed this with @shuding, we decided that it'd be nice if the request ran to completion (and wasn't aborted), even if the result is discarded by the router.

You don't need to abort the request, you just need to make sure that once the action resolves it doesn't override the state of the router. Otherwise if they resolve out of order you'll get the wrong final state.

For example, one way to do this is to set an `aborted` flag on the action object. Then in `handleResult`, check if the action was aborted before applying the state.

In a otel setup (in an application, not in Next), you could do something like this:

```
traceProvider.register({
  propagator: new XPropagator(),
})
```

E.g. you could use [`AWSXRayPropagator`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js-contrib/blob/main/propagators/opentelemetry-propagator-aws-xray/src/AWSXRayPropagator.ts) or make your own.

This propagator could work off headers or some special environment context. Next.js wouldn't need to know any of that - it'd just call a generic `propagator.extract()` and  (eventually)`propagator.inject()` and delegate this part fully to the configuration of the application or a deployment environment.

author: styfle

body:
Even with promises-based fs APIs, the main thread is still blocked by `await` in the single-threaded script, effectively idling (`install-native.mjs` is a single-thread script, invoked by `pnpm run`). 

fs async APIs are favored when the main thread should not be blocked, such as a web server managing several incoming requests, or using `Promise.all` to parallelize tasks sent in the Node.js's libuv worker pool. But we are not doing those in `install-native.mjs`.

Generally, fs sync APIs are faster (up to 40%) than async APIs (They don't require creating Promise objects, which alleviates GC pressure and avoids extra ticks).

body:
TLDR: this custom package takes on the responsibilities of the original class, providing a concise API for the user.

Since the API implies replacing the original FileSystemCache class with a custom one, it is not enough to replace the Map with the Redis Client from [the example in the docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/next-config-js/incrementalCacheHandlerPath). In this case, reading pre-rendered pages from disk will be lost. You can see [that my tests is failing](https://github.com/caching-tools/next-shared-cache/actions/runs/6764512665/job/18382888425?pr=94#step:9:240) if I restrict file system access. The library implements work with the file system. So, when Redis fails, the applications in pods will continue to work with the file system until Redis is online.

Also, for the correct operation of on-demand revalidation, you must have a common TagsManifest for all pods. Since tagsManifest is checked in [this](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/31c2f976cdd4deb0e7c412538a70b795dff4689e/packages/next/src/server/lib/incremental-cache/file-system-cache.ts#L255) and [this](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/31c2f976cdd4deb0e7c412538a70b795dff4689e/packages/next/src/server/lib/incremental-cache/file-system-cache.ts#L275) places in the original class, it is necessary to support this functionality.

This functionality is the same for everyone and is, therefore, encapsulated in the library.

In an ideal world, I would like to have such an API for customizing caching out of the box, and I would be willing to spend the effort and time to implement this for Next.js since, in essence, my library is inspired mainly by your implementation.

body:
Hey @leerob 

This is a really welcome change, I've been really looking forward to have something like this. One question here, does this approach cover the use case of using the env vars within client components? To elaborate, we have had cases where our entire page is a client component, and within the page we are using client-facing env variables. Since Next.js bundles the `NEXT_PUBLIC` variables at build time, there is no way for us to use browser-facing variables on the client.

One example of using this - we have a Playwright test suite - our thinking was to do a `next build`, then locally start that build, perform e2e tests on that build output (I know that Playwright has a dev server option, we strictly want to execute tests on the build output to mimic the production environment as best as possible), and then after the tests are done, just convert that build into a docker image and deploy to production. With the current approach, this requires to create a new Next.js build output every time the environment variables change, which means in this case we have to create two builds instead of reusing the one.

It might be worth including a rudimentary example documenting how this would be solved. For example, Remix docs simply suggest to use the loaders to fetch it from the server and then expose it to the browser, pretty much like we had with `getServerSideProps` in the Pages Router. It would be really beneficial to explain how to do this with the App Router. Is the solution to just wrap that piece of client-side code in a server component and perform the fetching in that server component? What approach do you recommend in this case?

There's one important use case missing - when `getStaticProps` are used without ISR, then the default headers are similar to immutable assets (`s-maxage=31536000, stale-while-revalidate`), with aggressive cache headers set for long cache storage on CDN.

And given that page URLs are not changing with each deploy, customers who self-host Next.js will have scenarios of stale cache on their CDN's, without ability to override cache longevity settings for such pages.

This is where having control over `cache-control` headers would be very useful, but currently it's overridden by Next.js in production.

body:
In React we just write `val !== undefined`. (Don’t need to do the typeof thing in strict mode). It’s faster than calling a helper function because you don’t have an extra stack frame.

A function might compress better in some cases (although not always) but the way to think code size is that it’s mostly a heuristic for how long it takes for the VM to parse and compile (that’s why byte for byte JS is way more expensive than, say, an image); in this case the inlined form is very simple.

author: feedthejim

body:
I've called out in the description that this pattern _should_ be used again, and used frequently within the codebase. There's too many situations where we are don't have timeouts set in order to enforce a "fail fast, fail early" approach rather than waiting for something like a lambda timeout to occur. This helps keep costs lower for users who are taking advantage of serverless.

In this specific case, the headers being flushed is something that React doesn't specifically guarantee at the return time of the promise. That may be resolved in the future, where it doesn't have to wait until the response is piped, but this pattern ensures that we don't encounter this in the future.

I'm also a strong proponent of creating these abstractions, as they're single responsibility, and don't unnecessarily bloat the already huge function with more custom logic that'll be harder to refactor and digest, and more importantly, test. The abstraction here let me isolate this behavior and write tests to cover the use cases of it so we don't have to guess as to it's effectiveness within the E2E environment.
author: wyattjoh

body:
> I'm also a strong proponent of creating these abstractions, as they're single responsibility, and don't unnecessarily bloat the already huge function with more custom logic that'll be harder to refactor and digest, and more importantly, test.

To be fair, it's easy to say these are easy to digest when you're the one that wrote them 😆 You're essentially proposing that we maintain our own internal "lodash"-like utility library. Which is fair enough but we shouldn't be landing these as part of a bugfix.

My objection as a PR reviewer is that I've never come across this utility function before, so now in order to properly review this bugfix, I gotta go familiarize myself with your utility functions. Then I gotta decide whether adding these functions is worth the abstraction overhead.

At the very least, I think adding a new utility like this should be in a separate PR so as a team we can decide together whether to add to our "lodash library".

FWIW, in general, I personally dislike these kinds of small utility functions just as strongly as you seem to prefer them 😆 Because in most cases I find the expanded code easier to read than the abstraction. And I actually find it easier to refactor later, not harder, because all the code is in one place and it's easier to see which branches are no longer necessary. I don't have to wonder whether there's some crucial regression case that's only captured via a unit test of the function I want to replace. I'm not 100% anti-unit test in all cases... but probably like 99%. I've too often seen it become a crutch to give up on writing a proper e2e test.

But this is the kind of debate that belongs in a team meeting, or a separate PR that's focused just on these functions.

So my suggestion would be, could you extract this part of your PR into a separate PR that's stacked on top? That way we can review and land your fix and continue the debate later.

Because the enablement of PPR is dependant on the runtime + page kind, the `experimental` object was added to `RenderOpts` within app, enabling us to scope down the usage of renderOpts to specific page types. Ideally, we'd want to scope down access of each of the config options to each of the specific route implementaitons and runtimes.

In the most ideal world, we wouldn't pass around these huge bag-of-properties and instead rely on DI/IOC to isolate the configuration passing to the specific functions/classes/modules that require specific information from the configuration/render layers. That would solve the problem of PPR changes leaking into and breaking pages running inside `pages/`.

body:
```suggestion
      height={
        formattedProps.height !== '' ? formattedProps.height ?? null : null
      }
      width={formattedProps.width !== '' ? formattedProps.width ?? null : null}
```

Changing from `||` to `??` creates invalid CSS when empty strings are passed for `height` or `width`\. Since `GoogleMapsEmbed` accepts `height?: number | string`\, passing an empty string \(`""`\) will result in `height: "px"` instead of `height: "auto"`\.


<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## Empty strings passed to GoogleMapsEmbed produce invalid CSS

**What fails\:** `GoogleMapsEmbed` in `packages/third-parties/src/google/google-maps-embed.tsx` uses the nullish coalescing operator \(`??`\) to pass `height` and `width` to `ThirdPartyScriptEmbed`\. When an empty string is passed \(valid per the `height?: number | string` type\)\, it flows through to `ThirdPartyScriptEmbed` which generates invalid CSS\: `height: "px"` instead of `height: "auto"`\.

**How to reproduce\:**

```tsx
import { GoogleMapsEmbed } from '@next/third-parties/google'

// Empty strings are valid per the type definition
<GoogleMapsEmbed
  apiKey="test"
  mode="place"
  height=""
  width=""
/>
```

**Result\:** The generated style becomes `{ height: "px", width: "px" }` which is invalid CSS\.

**Expected\:** Empty strings should be treated like null\/undefined and result in `{ height: "auto", width: "auto" }`\.

**Root cause\:** The change from `||` to `??` operator in [commit 8e1a7724c9](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/8e1a7724c915e5248924255abe8e37acdbf27944) preserved `0` values but also preserved empty strings\, which are not nullish values\.

**Fix\:** Explicitly check for empty strings\: `height !== '' ? height ?? null : null` to handle all cases correctly\:

*   Empty string `""` → `null` → `height: "auto"` ✓
*   Number `0` → `0` → `height: "0px"` ✓
*   Valid strings\/numbers → preserved ✓
*   `null`\/`undefined` → `null` → `height: "auto"` ✓

</details>

body:
One example I have is about things that are not submitted via buttons. For example a checkbox that mutates the data when toggling:

```js
<input type="checkbox" onChange={async (e) => {
  await action(e.target.value)
}}/>
```

That's useful for optimistic forms. Same for `type="select"`, `type="radio"` and `type="input"` (e.g. auto-saving content with input debouncing) or even `<textarea>`s.

Another general use case with event handlers is for use cases that are usually not related to "forms", like triggering actions on `hover` events for advertising purposes. I don't have specific example here though but the ability is necessary.

For `useEffect`, the action might be depending on some global events:
- `onKeyDown` if you are adding keyboard shortcuts to your app. Imaging pressing `L` to like a tweet.
- `onScroll` for infinite loading related UX.

Or just triggered automatically, e.g. when this component is rendered (or the user has stayed for more than 5 minutes), increase the view counter in the DB.

```suggestion
While Server Actions in Next.js are primarily used for mutations (like POST, PUT, DELETE operations), they also play a crucial role in cache management. After a mutation, it's crucial to ensure that the cached data reflects the latest state. Next.js facilitates this by providing APIs such as [`revalidatePath`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) and [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag). These APIs can be used to purge or revalidate the cache immediately after a mutation. This capability ensures that any changes made by Server Actions are promptly reflected in the cached data, maintaining data consistency and accuracy.
```

Hmm this is odd....
For me: 
Zone B Calls Zone A

Zone A nextserver is hit:
```
       const isHMRRequestForHostApp =
          !basePath && req.url.startsWith('/_next/webpack-hmr') // returns false

        const isHMRRequestForGuestApp = pathHasPrefix(req.url, basePath) // returns true
```

which then means:
```
const isHMRRequestForCurrentBasepath =
          isHMRRequestForHostApp || isHMRRequestForGuestApp // becomes true in zone A because isHMRRequestForGuestApp is true
```

which then triggers:
```
    if (isHMRRequestForCurrentBasepath) {

> Listener functions **must** only perform **synchronous** operations. The Node.js process will exit immediately after calling the `'exit'` event listeners causing any additional work still queued in the event loop to be abandoned.

body:
Not actually being used yet but this is going to help us distinguish the following cases

1. SSR or RSC postpone that was caught and not rethrown
2. SSR postpone handled by React
3. RSC postpone handled by React

previously we could detect postpones in SSR by virtue of the prerender rerturning some postponed state but the other cases appear identical. Since we need to support case 3 we need to distinguish this and we are going to use the information about whether Next initiated a Postpone paired with the whether React handled that postpone to tell these cases apart.

Side note: with the use of onPostpone we can get much more granular with our warning about catching postpones. Right now we'd not warn if the render still postponed even if your code did handle catch and hide one of the Next postpones. Ideally we'd warn if a single postpone was intercepted regardless of whether the render ultimately still postponed. I'll leave that exercise for a later time though

  "include": [

    ".next/types/**/*.ts",

author: huozhi

body:
The `exit` event is sent right before the process exits and it can only execute synchronous code. I suppose we could capture it if we wanted to force the exit code to be `0`, but I was thinking letting it send the code it got made sense. 
https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-exit

> There is no way to prevent the exiting of the event loop at this point, and once all `'exit'` listeners have finished running the Node.js process will terminate.

> Listener functions **must** only perform **synchronous** operations. The Node.js process will exit immediately after calling the `'exit'` event listeners causing any additional work still queued in the event loop to be abandoned.

Since `server.close` is asychronous, I don't think calling it on the `'exit'` event would do anything useful

https://nodejs.org/api/net.html#serverclosecallback

> This function is asynchronous

I could see there maybe being a couple things that `server.close` does synchronously, but it definitely would exit without calling the callback.

```

@timneutkens after upgrading from `14.0.4` to `14.1.0` I'm seeing errors from this line when using Microsoft's `@azure/msal-browser` with NextJS. Specifically the error is:

`null is not an object (evaluating 'window.history.state.__PRIVATE_NEXTJS_INTERNALS_TREE')`

The flow that causes the error is that Microsoft has just redirected a user to my site with a hash in the URL, and the client code on my site (via the `@azure/msal-browser` package) is trying to remove the hash from the URL. Specifically, this line is being called:

https://github.com/AzureAD/microsoft-authentication-library-for-js/blob/2d4d0b2cde8e072ba6c64aea9b251984b2dd4021/lib/msal-browser/src/utils/BrowserUtils.ts#L21-L25

I have a patch locally that "fixes" this by adding `if (window.history.state == null) return;` directly above `startTransition(() => { ...` a couple of lines above here, but I don't understand Next.js's internals well enough to know if that's the right fix. I can submit a PR with it if you think it is.

❤️ for all your work on Next.js.

It's a little off to frame it as a _choice_ between `<video>` and `<iframe>` when it's really all about the hosting approach you're choosing. If you're self-hosting on cloud storage or a video API you're not going to use an iframe to play the video in your Next app, you're gonna use `<video>`. You could frame it as embedding video files versus embedding video service iframes/players.

body:
```suggestion
When incrementally migrating from `pages/` to `app/`, the Next.js router will automatically handle hard navigation between the two. To detect transitions from `pages/` to `app/`, there is a client router filter that leverages probabilistic checking of app routes, which can occasionally result in false positives. By default, such occurrences should be very rare, as we configure the false positive likelihood to be 0.01%. This likelihood can be customized via the `experimental.clientRouterFilterAllowedRate` option in `next.config.js`. It's important to note that lowering the false positive rate will increase the size of the generated filter in the client bundle.
```
author: samcx

body:
```suggestion
Alternatively, if you prefer to disable this handling completely and manage the routing between `pages/` and `app/` manually, you can set `experimental.clientRouterFilter` to false in `next.config.js`. When this feature is disabled, any dynamic routes in pages that overlap with app routes won't be navigated to properly by default.
```

body:
Removing this breaks the functionality that allows middleware to rewrite `_next/data` paths for a different project/deployment. 

Instead of changing this, we should ensure we 404 properly after middleware is invoked, we didn't rewrite/redirect, and the buildId doesn't match at that point.
author: ijjk

body:
First, I am sorry about the failing test cases. I tried to get `pnpm build` and `pnpm test-start` working in 3 different envs (macOS (with volta installed), the repo's devcontainer, and a ubuntu VM) with `pnpm build` complaining about missing dependencies after `pnpm i`).

> Instead of changing this, we should ensure we 404 properly after middleware is invoked, we didn't rewrite/redirect, and the buildId doesn't match at that point.

But the case of a successful rewrite is the culprit here. next.js needs to properly 404 after middleware is invoked, the `buildId` is different and a rewrite happened.

Clicking `Link` after a deployment with a different `buildId` will do the following:
Request to `_next/data/....json` is made with:
```
'x-middleware-prefetch': '1'
'x-nextjs-data': '1'
```

Middleware will rewrite that and will add
```
'x-invoke-path': '',
'x-invoke-query': '',
'x-invoke-output': '',
'x-middleware-invoke': '1'
```
before `normalizeAndAttachMetadata` and thus `handleNextDataRequest` is called.

Based on these headers the issue is in the branch where `handleCatchallRenderRequest` is called.
I am not sure if this is the only branch that is affected, though, as I am not very familiar with "middleware to rewrite _next/data paths for a different project/deployment."

What about letting `normalizeAndAttachMetadata` return `[complete, buildIdMismatch]`, and before `handleCatchallRenderRequest` check if `buildIdMismatch` is true and render 404 in that case before executing `handleCatchallRenderRequest`?


I can provide a reproducible case if you want.

body:
You can add a new section called **Params** to show the arguments the default export / middleware function accepts (req). Here's an example from the other file API references: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#props. But we should use `Params` instead of `Props` because it's a function.

It might be worth noting a small quirk that usually throws people off. When importing `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`, they look similar, but one is a type and the other is a class. 

Since the `request` is passed to the default function, we give it the type, `NextRequest` . e.g. `export async function middleware(request: NextRequest)`.

`NextResponse`, on the other hand, is imported and used within the function, but not passed.

I believe we want the stale-while-revalidate delta to always be at least a year as this is the amount of time a cache is allowed to keep the stale value and if a resource is failing to revalidate we don't want to evict the stale content just as fast as we want to revalidate the content.

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: type-safety -->
The function parameter type is missing `MetadataRoute.SitemapIndex`, causing a type safety issue when handling sitemap-index data.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
The `resolveRouteData` function accepts a `fileType` parameter that includes `'sitemap-index'`, but the `data` parameter type union only includes `MetadataRoute.Robots | MetadataRoute.Sitemap | MetadataRoute.Manifest`. It's missing `MetadataRoute.SitemapIndex`. This creates a type safety gap where the function can be called with sitemap-index data but TypeScript won't catch potential type mismatches.

When `fileType` is `'sitemap-index'`, the function casts `data` to `MetadataRoute.SitemapIndex` on line 126, but TypeScript has no guarantee that the input data actually conforms to this type.

---

### Recommendation
Update the `data` parameter type on line 112 to include `MetadataRoute.SitemapIndex`:

```typescript
data: MetadataRoute.Robots | MetadataRoute.Sitemap | MetadataRoute.Manifest | MetadataRoute.SitemapIndex,
```
</details>

<!-- VADE-CATEGORY: other -->
Function name `sitemapIndex()` is misleading since it returns `MetadataRoute.Sitemap`, not a sitemap index.

<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
The function is named `sitemapIndex()` but it returns `MetadataRoute.Sitemap` and generates a regular sitemap with individual page URLs (home and about pages). This naming is confusing because:

1. The function name suggests it's creating a sitemap index (which references other sitemaps)
2. But it's actually creating a regular sitemap with page URLs
3. The actual sitemap-index functionality is in `sitemap-index.ts`

This inconsistency could confuse developers using this example as a reference.

---

### Recommendation
Rename the function from `sitemapIndex()` to `sitemap()` to accurately reflect that it's generating a regular sitemap, not a sitemap index:

```typescript
export default function sitemap(): MetadataRoute.Sitemap {
```
</details>
