body:
was talking to Wyatt about this today. We probably want to make this into a map so we can just look up by digest.

We also should make sure that our digests are unique. At least for anything that goes into allCapturedErrors. This may already be the case b/c the redirect and notFound errors may be omitted (I haven't looked closely yet). However there is a case where I think we could still get the same digest for multiple onError calls. When you abort a react render all the suspense boundaries still pending are marked for client render and each one results in an onError call. But since the error object will be the same in each case it will produce an identical digest. We actually would have a component stack in dev and when prerendering which can make them unique again but it won't help with regular renders in prod. Perhaps we just add a bit of entropy to the digest on each onError calls since we know each call to onError represents a unique error even if the error value is shared.
author: gnoff

body: consider also looking for the component stack on the second arg `errorInfo` which will exist in Dev and during prerenders in prod
author: gnoff

body:
Continuing on the reasons why a map might be better in this case...

I'd expect that if an error occurs, because the error digest is unique, we should not insert into the map if the digest already exists. This is really important, as different renderers may be handed the "masked" error rather than the underlying error first. For example:

1. Original `RedirectError` is thrown, containing a digest of `NEXT_REDIRECT;replace;/some/url;303;`
2. Add error to error map with the digest as the key
3. The `onError` returns this digest, which is later consumed by other layers, which in turn is caught by it's `onError` handler

In this case, the first occurrence of the error should be the one that is the original error, not any subsequent ones. _Technically_, your code here works, but that's only because _new_ errors are pushed into the array, and the `.find()` will get the _first_ occurrence of that digest.

body:
Fair, although arguably we should rather work towards getting rid of as many of the current config/build files as possible, instead of planning on adding more.

I think if we added even more config/build files, at that point, a `config` folder would then be justifiable and we could just ignore a single folder instead. Accidentally publishing a config file - then excluding it in a follow-up release - is probably less of a DX hit than forgetting to include an actual submodule anyway.

Working with the 50+ files contained in this root directory however is increasingly frictional, and these files could technically just be generated anyway, as they are just static aliases to other files that are currently spread out non-systematically. This can be addressed in a follow-up PR though.

This PR aims to be a - maybe somewhat opinionated, but hopefully positive - small DX improvement as a stopgap on the way to properly supporting the `exports` field for submodules anyway, which is the current standard for managing submodule paths.

Our tests should also fail if someone tried importing `next/dist/*` which currently isn't the case, because even we misuse these import paths.

In light of this, feel free to close or merge this PR. :pray:

## Custom Components and `<Link />`

When using the `<Link />` component with a custom component that wraps an `<a>` tag, ensure that the behavior aligns with your expectations. Below is an example:

```jsx
<AppOnly>
  <!-- Your custom component content here -->
</AppOnly>

// The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page.
<Link href="/some-page">
  <!-- Link content here -->
</Link>
`


Middleware is commonly employed for tasks such as authentication or user redirection to different pages. When using Middleware and <Link /> together, it's important to consider prefetching links to avoid unnecessary fetches. Provide both the display URL and the prefetch URL to Next.js, as demonstrated below:


// Middleware Usage Example
import Link from 'next/link';

// In your component
<Link href="/some-page" as="/custom-route" prefetch>
  <!-- Link content here -->
</Link>
``

body:
The benefit that `@mdx-js/react` offers, is that it allows users to provide components for MDX files for different files in the React tree. IMO this is a niche use case. I think the `mdx-components` file is a much better solution for Next.js. Kudos to whoever came up with that.

`@mdx-js/react` works for the pages directory, but not for the app directory. It just crashes with a weird error. I personally found this confusing and I’ve heard so from others too.

Regardless of what works or doesn’t work, IMO it’s good to have a single blessed way to use MDX with Next.js. I think it’s hard to explain what the type of router has to do with this.

Using the `mdx-components` file better aligns with the DX after I implement [support for provided components](https://github.com/mdx-js/mdx-analyzer/issues/399) in the MDX language server. Just define them once globally, then use them in every MDX file.

What is missing from this PR though, is the addition of the `mdx-components` file. I could add it, but even better would be to merge #59693.

Isn't it a little confusing to cache for a long time when `true`?
How about allowing a default `staletime` to be set instead of a boolean?
author: AkifumiSato

body: @AkifumiSato thanks for the feedback! This is something we've discussed a bit internally as well. If you were given the ability to customize this value globally, what would you set it to and could you share a bit about how you decided on that particular number?
author: ztanner

body:
Thanks for the quick reply. If numbers can be set, I would consider these four patterns to determine the value.

- `0`: Completely off
- `5`: Enabled for only a short time
- `30`(default): Not care particularly
- `86400` ~ `31556952000`: Very long time.

Now, I can't set `5`. This case, I want to enable the cache for high performance, but only for very short time that are not stressful to the user. (However, I am concerned that setting `1` will cause self DDos.)
I also think it will be clear that `86400` ~ `31556952000` is a long lifetime, unlike true.
What do you think?
author: AkifumiSato

body:
I see -- I'm curious about the difference between 30 seconds and 5 seconds for what you're describing. The time values seem very close together and seems like a difference of 25 seconds would be imperceptible to the end-user when clicking around. 

The primary goal of this flag is to let users experiment with opting out of the router cache entirely as it's been a source of frequent feedback. This flag in it's current form will most likely not be stabilized, as we have other ideas for how to solve the caching feedback. So rather than introduce another time value that the user has to think about, we wanted to keep the opt-out behavior simple.
author: ztanner

body:
For me, 5 seconds is very different from 30 seconds, but I think this is a matter of stress sensation and difficult to explain logically. However, I can very much understand the primary focus on opt-outs in response to community feedback.
But then I was wondering about the difference in behavior between undefined and true, so I commented. Is it necessary to distinguish between `undefined` / `true`?
author: AkifumiSato

body: `true` would be if you wanted to keep the browser cache around for the entire session (a bit closer to a SPA-like app) whereas `undefined` would be to keep the existing behavior without any unexpected changes.
author: ztanner

body:
Is the `true` behavior something that was in the feedback from the community? Are there many people who want `true`?
Personally, I just thought `false` or `ture` would be easier to understand, and I have no problem with the current behavior. If this is what you need, please do not go through my comments. Thanks for discussing!
author: AkifumiSato

body: The majority of the feedback has been a way to disable it, though we have seen interest in the long-lived cache. This lets people experiment with both while we collect feedback. Just to reiterate, we don't expect this to become a stabilized API in NextConfig.

I'd enqueue more than one chunk. what we expect is to reproduce the server inserted html on each chunk. This currently makes sense because we always precede this transform with one that creates a buffered chunk of an entire set of HTML that React is trying to flush. Crazy idea here but what if we keep the transpiled source in memory and then we import it via a data URL e.g.

```js
import(`data:text/javascript,${transpiledSource}`)

body:
For consideration:

Generally I'd prefer we not build general utilities when we don't actually need their generic power. In this case the indexOf will only ever be searching for a few very specific and special byte sequences so we can ship a faster implementation that doesn't have to work in every case.

In chat we talked about how we really should match `<body>` or `<body ` instead of `<body` because the latter could match a custom element that starts with body. but doing this doubles the search because we now need to scan twice when really what we want is a sequence where the last byte can be one of two different values.

We could land this but it would just temp us to continue using this general tool which might make it hard to improve upon later

author: gnoff

body:
For consideration:

in practice React will always flush the closing body and html tag at the very end in it's own chunk which means that most of the time the chunk you will be removing these closing tags will only contain those tags. You could probably do a fast path where `tagIndex === 0` leads to `return chunk.subarray(b.length)` so you avoid copying
author: gnoff

body:
This could actually be slower because string concat can be very fast whereas this is repeatedly copying ever growing buffers.

I'd recommend that you just push all the chunks into an array and then in the flush call you copy them all into a single chunk and then search for the desired tags there. It's close enough to the existing implementation I'd argue there is trivial risk of changing semantics and it will not have adverse perf characteristics the larger the page

would be better IMO to type this as `IncomingMessage` since it's only used in one place and it's not a safe general purpose URL validator.

We can also get rid of the origin checks because the IncomingMessage url does not contain a host value. I'm curious why this was added in the original implementation. body:
TypeScript didn't care to reference `misc.d.ts` in reachable declaration files for some reason. Now it does so we have two options:
1. Force the old behavior by not referencing `misc.d.ts` at all
2. Get rid of the two-world type-checking where internally we emit declarations with `misc.d.ts` but then publicly rely on `compiled.d.ts` existing in the program

Point 2 is quite involved since it requires having either the same types for internal and public or at least public types that are compatible with internal types. Right now, the public types are not compatible with the internal types (e.g. you can't redeclare a value even though its type is `any`). We'd have to inline Webpack types which is quite involved (mostly because there's no tool to bundle types, see https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/4433).

In this PR I choose 1. by rewriting references to `$$compiled.internal.d.ts` (the old `misc.d.ts`) to `compiled.d.ts`. This has the benefit of more clearly communicating what `misc.d.ts` and `compiled.d.ts` actually represented.

That the rewrite is sound (or at least as sound as prior typings were) is ensured by the new typechecking tests from https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64478 and all the existing tests including type-checking.

body:
> Is that when you click the "Update Branch" button or is it when the PR is merged to canary?

When the GitHub actions job is created which simulates "when the PR is merged to canary" 

It doesn't run on the head commit on the branch (i.e. what you would run the tests on) but on the commit of the merge branch. The GH Actions docs try to explain this:
> Note that GITHUB_SHA for this event is the last merge commit of the pull request merge branch. If you want to get the commit ID for the last commit to the head branch of the pull request, use github.event.pull_request.head.sha instead.

In https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/8605523039/job/23581990844?pr=64117#step:27:30 you can see that `HEAD~1` is sufficient. I cherry-picked this PR onto https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64117 and diffing against `HEAD~1` got all changes of the branch that consisted of 4 commits.

Imagine you have this history:
```
A-B-C-main
 \
  D-E-branch
```

By default, GH Actions will not check out the `branch` ref (i.e. the head of the branch). Instead, it will merge `branch` into `main` and then run on that commit:

```
A-B-C-main - F
 \          /
  D-E-branch
```
F is the commit GH actions (i.e. `actions/checkout`) checks out by default.

In that scenario diffing against `HEAD~1` will be sufficient to include all changes that are exclusive to the branch (since it just includes the merge commit) whereas diffing against `main` would include all the changes exclusive to `branch` *and* all the changes on `main` since `branch` was forked. I don't see how including changes in B and C in CI for PRs is helpful.

You can also see this behavior in the logs of `actions/checkout`: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/8605588371/job/23582826423?pr=64218#step:9:93
This is the log for GH Actions of this PR. The head commit is 9e87c4ce2fedcfd8275e9108523ed1e2a0d12df0 i.e. the commit `HEAD` would point to if you'd check out this branch locally. However, in CI, `HEAD` points to `dda5fbd7` which is the merge commit of merging 9e87c4ce2fedcfd8275e9108523ed1e2a0d12df0 into its fork point with `canary` (`f9ad49fc6f57f3bcf4f508b59deab695f06c74b1`): 
> HEAD is now at dda5fbd7 Merge 9e87c4ce2fedcfd8275e9108523ed1e2a0d12df0 into f9ad49fc6f57f3bcf4f508b59deab695f06c74b1

The DefinitelyTyped repo is using the exact same strategy: https://github.com/DefinitelyTyped/DefinitelyTyped/blame/master/scripts/pnpm-install.sh#L22

body:
In general, it is beneficial to propagate sampled and un-sampled contexts because telemetry systems often do traced-based sampling, where a tracing decision for a particular trace (usually decided on the first service) is propagated across the entire system, and the individual services of the system only report spans, if the incoming tracing decision is positive.

For example in the `traceparent` header there is a flag indicating whether the trace is sampled or not: https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/#sampled-flag If we didn't propagate the data when the trace is not sampled, the flag would not be needed in the first place.

Does that make sense? All in all this is good because it allows us to have less logic here. :)

body:
I was checking what will the propagation data can be used, seems not all of them will be used for rendering injected metadata. Some could be used in request/response headers. Maybe we should give everything a prefix for categorizing. Then a propagation data key's format is `<category>@<key>`, for example `metadata@` can be the prefix.

To inject metadata rendering tags we can use  `metadata@meta-tag-key` as key and `the-value` as value for identify it's for metadata. We'll filter the ones starting with `metadata@` for injecting meta tags.

If we need to use propagation data for other cases, we can add a different category, such as `headers@key` and `value` as k-v pair propagation data for injecting headers.
author: huozhi

body:
Trying to sum up my thoughts (and also our slack convo):

Long story short, I think adding something like a `namespace@` would not work for the use case I was attempting to fix with this PR and would be mixing too many concepts.

Generally speaking, OpenTelemetry users have a convention for the name of the keys in their propagation data. Having a `metadata@` prefix would mess with that convention. When implementing an OpenTelemetry `Propagator`, you cannot know at runtime whether your data will be `inject`ed into a meta tag or attached as headers to outgoing requests. Having the `metadata@` prefix in headers of outgoing requests would certainly be problematic in many cases.

I do agree with the fact that Next.js probably needs a way to dynamically attach response headers. However, I don't think using OpenTelemetry is the right vehicle for that. Returning trace information to the client as response headers is generally of no use, because you cannot extract it with JS (except for very few exceptions like `Server-Timing`). I suggest that if you guys want to add a mechanism to return response headers you add it through a more explicit API.

body:
This change does not look correct to me.
The intent of next-polyfill-module and next-polyfill-nomodule is to ensure compat with the supported browsers: https://nextjs.org/docs/architecture/supported-browsers.
These browsers are specifically chosen as they're the cutoff point of `module`/`nomodule` support (ES Modules support). So the built-in polyfill that are loaded in all browsers, and the polyfills that are only loaded in browsers that don't support ES Modules, are specifically tuned to support the APIs that the ES Modules browsers had at the time, not to load all polyfills, as that would mean Next.js will forever keep increasing the polyfill size whenever new browser features are added, that's not something we want, i.e. we don't want to have to load a polyfill for `toReversed` in all browsers because the older version of ES Modules browsers also doesn't have it.

Our recommendation for these newer features is to pull in the polyfills as you need them / want to use them. In this case you need to load the `toReversed` polyfill for all browsers, even ones that support it, as there is no way to conditionally load it like `nomodule`.

Hope that clarifies 🙏

author: styfle

body:
Given the `"next": "canary"` dependency in `package.json` in the reproduction templates, `pnpm update next` updates next to the latest canary version (pinned) at that time:

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/assets/1935696/2bbcfbfc-bee0-4cd7-ab15-dca3b70a44fe
author: karlhorky

body:
Any further executions of `pnpm update next` will not upgrade the version any further than the pinned version caused by the first run of `pnpm update next`.

This means that the specific canary version number will be tied to the forked reproduction sandbox, which is often wanted for reproducibility and avoids the following issue:

1.⁠ User creates a reproduction on a certain canary version
2.⁠ ⁠⁠New canary version is released
3.⁠ ⁠⁠User restarts the `dev` task for any reason
4.⁠ ⁠⁠Next.js version updated, potentially leading to the bug disappearing from the reproduction (URL may be published somewhere publicly) 💥
author: karlhorky

Unfortunately this is hard to do correctly. We substitute these in a slightly incorrect way, where DefineEnvPlugin will turn `process.env.__NEXT_AFTER` into a boolean, not a string. So if we wanted to be explicit here, it'd need to be `process.env.__NEXT_AFTER === true`, and that'll rightfully anger typescript, which expects `process.env` to contain strings. Getting around this using `!!` is unfortunately pretty common across the codebase.

I'd also prefer to clean this up, but doing this properly should be a codebase-wide cleanup, so let's do that in a another PR.
author: lubieowoce

body:
Unfortunately this doesn't seem possible today outside of edge enviroments.

For edge, we have an internal `NextFetchEvent` (with a proxy `waitUntil`), and we return the promises from that as part of a  `FetchEventResult`. Then, its consumer is expected to call the platform-specifc `waitUntil` (see e.g. the handler produced by `vc build` doing that [here](https://github.com/vercel/vercel/blob/14059906d312a683044acc4cd1ff3b49e2e7c837/packages/next/src/edge-function-source/get-edge-function.ts#L133)).

...but there's nothing equivalent to that that we can do for `nodejs`. I'm also not a fan of having vercel-specific code in here, but that seems to be the best we can do right now. I'd leave improvements to this as a follow-up if that's okay.

(I think the ideal solution would be to inject the the platform-specific `waitUntil` from `vc build`, either by stashing it on `req/res` or by wrapping the handler in another ALS, but one that's defined by Next. that'd also make integration easier for non-vercel use-cases.)

Here are the 19.0 versions in ASCII sort order

```
  "19.0.0-beta-1beb73de0f-20240503",
  "19.0.0-beta-4508873393-20240430",
  "19.0.0-beta-5d29478716-20240506",
  "19.0.0-beta-73bcdfbae5-20240502",
  "19.0.0-beta-94eed63c49-20240425",
  "19.0.0-beta-b498834eab-20240506",
```
You can see that it's not necessarily in chronological order.

[semver.org](https://semver.org/) section 11.4.2 says ASCII sort order will be used for each dot-separated section in the pre-release ID.

If react were to swap the hash and the date, I think your `^` range would mostly work. Except for multiple releases on the same date, like on `0506`.

body:
It doesn't really matter here, but you could change it to:

```suggestion
            let polyfill_output_asset =
                RawOutput::new(polyfill_output_path, polyfill_module);
```

If you give `RawOutput` an additional `path` argument, which it reports as `ident()` `AssetIdent::from_path(path)`. That would allow the `RawOutput` to "serve" a `Source` under a specific path.

---

The motivation behind that:

Eventually we want to have lazy compilation. That would mean instead of emitting all OutputAssets directly to disk we would directly serve them on request. That would mean `Asset::content()` on OutputAssets is only called when the file is actually requested. So we want to delay as much work as possible to this point. e. g. Chunks only generate the content in the `content()` method, so code generation is skipped until this point.
By having `RawOutput::new(polyfill_output_path, polyfill_module)` the `polyfill_module.content()` method would only be called when the file is requested. So that would cause the polyfill file not to be read until it's actually requested from the browser.

```js
const PARAMETER_PATTERN = /\[((?:\[.*\])|.+)\]/

We take the first match and pass that into `parseMatchedParameter` which in the example of `[[...foo]]` will be `[...foo]`.  Thats why `parseMatchedParameter` checks for `startsWith([)` and `endsWith(])` sets optional to `true`.  In the example of `[...foo]`, `parseMatchParameter` received `...foo` and thus is not marked as optional

This part makes me scratch my head. 

I'm not sure its necessary in this instance, but generally, when using `TextDecoder` in stream mode, you should always do one final call to `.decode()` with `stream:false` in order to ensure the final chunk has been decoded. Depending how `flightReader` is implemented, you could have a race condition where `value` is falsey the same time `done` is `false`, and then you may have chunks still inside of the decoder.

body:
So the approach of this PR is to generalize the not found and forbidden in an abstraction but this doesn't quite achieve what I was hoping we could/would. There is still a separate boundary for each of these functions when what we really want to achieve is a single boundary. We also ideally eventually would roll redirect boundary behavior into this component.

I went through the PR with @huozhi and he will end up doing more review and providing additional feedback. But one thing that this PR also needs before we can land is a more comprehensive test suite. The current one doesn't actually use `forbidden.ts` nor does it exercise the new methods in server actions and route handlers.

What I'd like to see is a removal of abstractions rather than the creation of new ones (ui-error-boundary and friends). But maybe before jumping into this work let's give @huozhi a chance to provide guidance or communicate a plan on what we will do internally before/after landing this

If we add support for notAuthorized too we'd have to add another. Can we unify these two into a single boundary? Maybe even include the redirect boundary as well so we eliminate some component tree depth

Found one case cannot pass, which is esm externals. When a client component became a promise because having async dependencies.

When accessing the layout or page component, we access the `.default` property which is the deep proxy to a Promise. React cannot handle it as a component.

body:
Thanks for nudging me to look closer, this is an interesting finding.

- The `navigation-types/compat/navigation.d.ts` file is included in the typescript program because there are e2e/integration tests that have `/// <reference types="next/navigation-types/compat/navigation" />`  in their `next-env.d.ts`. This will be [generated like that whenever there is both app dir and pages dir](https://github.com/wyattjoh/next.js/blob/16a0e5af3213c0078b3069c795bf2bdad202c896/test/unit/write-app-declarations.test.ts#L102-L111).
- The compiler error appeared only now because `tsc` didn't even do a full compilation before with the broken `BrowserInterface` class.
- The compiler error would also appear in a freshly created Next.js project that uses app dir and also has a pages route that imports from `next/navigation`, **_if_** `skipLibCheck` wouldn't be enabled by default.
- Here's a repro: https://github.com/unstubbable/next-navigation-types

So to summarise, you could consider this an accidental bugfix.

body:
```suggestion


> **Good to know:**
>
> - To display form errors in the user UI, you should return a **serializable object** instead of throwing an error (e.g. `throw new Error('...')`. Uncaught errors in Server Actions are considered to be an internal server error and the error message [will not be sent to the client](/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/error-handling#securing-sensitive-error-information) in production to avoid leaking sensitive information. See more information on [error handling](#error-handling) in Server Actions.
> - Throwing errors will trigger the nearest the nearest `error.js` boundary - see [Error Handling](/docs/app/building-your-application/data-fetching/server-actions-and-mutations#error-handling)
> - Before mutating data, you should always ensure a user is also authorized to perform the action. See [Authentication and Authorization](#authentication-and-authorization).
```

body:
I removed `"exclude": ["node_modules"]` in #66461 because it was not needed as it had no effect. As per the [docs](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#exclude):

> `exclude` only changes which files are included as a result of the [`include`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#include) setting. A file specified by `exclude` can still become part of your codebase due to an `import` statement in your code, a `types` inclusion, a `/// <reference` directive, or being specified in the [`files`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#files) list.
>
> It is not a mechanism that **prevents** a file from being included in the codebase - it simply changes what the [`include`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#include) setting finds.

You can verify that by running `pnpm typescript --listFiles | wc -l` with and without it.

Adding it here again does not change the compiler errors you mentioned, as far as I can see. You could only suppress them with `skipLibCheck`, which I hope we won't need to do, and can find a better solution instead. Maybe it should be raised in https://github.com/GoogleChrome/web-vitals that https://github.com/GoogleChrome/web-vitals/blob/main/src/types.ts now has conflicting types with `typescript@5.5.2/node_modules/typescript/lib/lib.dom.d.ts`.

PS: I couldn't answer to your question in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/66461#issuecomment-2184501593 because the PR is locked.

EDIT: Ah ok, you've raised it already: https://github.com/GoogleChrome/web-vitals/pull/497 👍

body:
What this PR tries to do is prevent hitting [this specific path](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/67257/files/a1f627d30eed6685c694b13c02ae7eb894fda56f#diff-07cdc7c577b57eb1e3cf336ecca5995abae754a39c20f5bba67794dece3ddf21R690-R718), with `optimizeImage` is the expensive operation.

`upstreamEtag` represents the original source image's etag (currently calculated via the same function `getImageEtag`), whereas the cache entry's `etag` represents the resulting image's `etag`, i.e. in the case image optimization is done, the `etag` will be the hash of that optimized image instead of the upstream image.

This condition exists to cause a revalidation on cases where the optimization did not happen previously (in this case we fallback to using `upstreamBuffer` and `upstreamEtag` for the image), so this will fail early on those cases and cause a new optimization attempt. Although now thinking back at it the likelyhood of the image optimization ending up with the same outcome is quite likely anyways.

When this condition is true, we'll check the next condition, comparing the previous upstream image's etag against the current upstream image's etag to determine if we should revalidate or not.
author: kahlstrm

body:
The optimization not happening could be because of a fallback (such as an error was thrown) or it could be because the image was vector form (svg doesnt need to be optimized). 

Either way, we still need to revalidate those images because the upstream response could have changed since the previous request. So I suggest removing line 463 and that way the following line (465) can actually compare the new upstream etag.

```suggestion
  regexp: string
  /** @default true */
  locale?: boolean
  has?: RouteHas[]
  missing?: RouteHas[]
  originalSource: string
```

The `ProxyMatcher` type definition has been incorrectly modified\. It removes the required `originalSource` field and adds an unused `source` field\, causing a mismatch with the implementation and breaking type compatibility throughout the codebase\.


<details>
<summary>View Details</summary>
<!-- PATCH_DETAILS_PLACEHOLDER -->

### Analysis
## ProxyMatcher type definition missing required fields

**What fails\:** The `ProxyMatcher` type definition in `packages/next/src/build/analysis/get-page-static-info.ts` \(lines 48\-55\) is missing the required `originalSource` field and has an incorrect `regexp` type\, causing type mismatches when the function returns values that don\'t match the declared type signature\. Code throughout the codebase attempts to access `originalSource` on ProxyMatcher instances\, which causes type errors\.

**How to reproduce\:**

1.  The `getMiddlewareMatchers()` function returns objects with\:
    
    ```typescript
    return {
      ...rest,
      regexp: tryToParsePath(result.data).regexStr!,  // Always returns regexp
      originalSource: originalSource || source,        // Always returns originalSource
    }
    ```
    
2.  Code in `packages/next/src/build/adapter/build-complete.ts:707` accesses the field\:
    
    ```typescript
    return {
      source: item.originalSource,  // Will type error - field doesn't exist in ProxyMatcher
      sourceRegex: item.regexp,
    }
    ```
    
3.  Code in `packages/next/src/shared/lib/turbopack/manifest-loader.ts:747` accesses it\:
    
    ```typescript
    matcher.regexp = safePathToRegexp(matcher.originalSource, [], ...)  // Type error
    ```
    
4.  Test expectations in `packages/next/src/build/analysis/get-page-static-info.test.ts` expect the field \(lines 9\, 22\, 27\)
    

**Result\:** Type mismatch \- functions return `originalSource: string` and `regexp: string` \(required\) but the type definition declares `regexp?: string` \(optional\) and no `originalSource` field

**Expected\:** ProxyMatcher type should define\:

```typescript
export type ProxyMatcher = {
  regexp: string
  locale?: boolean
  has?: RouteHas[]
  missing?: RouteHas[]
  originalSource: string
}
```

This matches the Rust struct definition in `crates/next-core/src/next_manifests/mod.rs:259` which defines `original_source: RcStr` as required\, and aligns with all actual usages throughout the codebase including `FunctionsConfigManifest` interface in `packages/next/src/build/index.ts:582`\.

</details>

### Analysis ## Missing TypeScript type definitions for compiled cookie module causes compilation errors **What fails\:** TypeScript compilation fails when trying to import `SerializeOptions` type from `next/dist/compiled/cookie` in `packages/next/src/server/api-utils/index.ts` \(line 3\) and `packages/next/src/server/api-utils/node/api-resolver.ts` \(line 5\)\. Error\: `Cannot find module 'next/dist/compiled/cookie' or its corresponding type declarations.` **How to reproduce\:** ```bash cd packages/next npx tsc --skipLibCheck false --noEmit src/server/api-utils/index.ts ``` **Result before fix\:** ``` src/server/api-utils/index.ts(3,39): error TS2307: Cannot find module 'next/dist/compiled/cookie' or its corresponding type declarations. src/server/api-utils/node/api-resolver.ts(5,39): error TS2307: Cannot find module 'next/dist/compiled/cookie' or its corresponding type declarations. ``` **Root cause\:** When the cookie package was upgraded from 0\.4\.1 to 1\.0\.2 \(commit 7270449519\)\, the type name changed from `CookieSerializeOptions` to `SerializeOptions`\. The npm `cookie@1.0.2` package now includes built\-in TypeScript definitions at `dist/index.d.ts` instead of relying on external `@types/cookie`\. However\, the build process that compiles the cookie module into `packages/next/src/compiled/cookie/` was not updated to copy the type definition file to the compiled module\. **Solution implemented\:** 1. Added `packages/next/src/compiled/cookie/index.d.ts` \- TypeScript type definitions copied from the npm cookie package 2. Updated `packages/next/src/compiled/cookie/package.json` to include `"types": "index.d.ts"` field 3. Enhanced `packages/next/taskfile-ncc.js` `writePackageManifest()` function to\: * Extract and preserve the `types` field from the original package\.json * Copy type definition files during the build process if they exist * Include the `types` field in the generated compiled package\.json This follows the same pattern used for other compiled packages like `@edge-runtime/ponyfill` which already include type definitions\.

We also already have a couple of other cases like that in `app-render`, e.g. `createServerInsertedHTML` or `getRequiredScripts`.  In this case, the main purpose is to reduce the clutter in the main function, and it's done in preparation for #67527 where I add the parsing of another header.

author: unstubbable

body:
I'm not opposed to pulling it into a separate, non-exported function to improve readability - `app-render` has a handful of functions in there that aren't used outside of it (ie `generateFlight` or `createFlightDataResolver`). My minor concern with it being moved into a separate module with a name like `parseRequestHeaders` is that it suggests that _this_ particular util is the way to parse request headers, but that's not entirely the case either. Once exported it's up for grabs and might start to be getting used in places where it shouldn't. For example, `base-server` pulls the data off of `requestMeta`:
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/5df4e7e83af3039823c560c9e7dab5066efacfce/packages/next/src/server/base-server.ts#L1937-L1946
author: ztanner

body:
Yeah that makes sense, though keep in mind that it's placed in `packages/next/src/server/app-render/`. But you're right, the function name sounds probably too generic. With auto-import you might end up in the situation you have in mind.

So the options are 1) inlining (although I'd like to get our modules smaller), 2) renaming (e.g. `getAppRenderContextFromHeaders` or something), or 3) discarding altogether (and reading the header in `withRequestStore`). Before moving forward, I think you need to take a look at #67527 because there the handling is changed a bit, and `parsedRequestHeaders` is added to `AppRenderBaseContext`.

For this case, I think to address the concerns of isolation and preventing creep, placing this function into the `app-render.tsx` as an unexported function would be best for now. I like the separate function over the inlining because it gives concrete types that can be described here, allowing good points for us to add comments/documentation to their uses and applications.

body:
We render multiple pages in parallel but each chunk is only loaded once in turbopack b/c React caches the module resolving promise internally. So if chunk A begins loading in page A and page B also loads it there won't be another call to the loader observable from within this file. So the only way to guarantee that we always load everything needed ahead of an SSR render is to wait globally for all pending chunks loading to finish before moving on to rendering the page. It's not ideal but it's not worth a "better" hack when we probably just need support for this in Turbopack.

FWIW this isn't a practical issue for webpack b/c on the server all the chunks are already loaded eagerly

body:
Yeah I agree it's a bit confusing.  Part of what's confusing is that prefetches are tightly coupled to navigations. A navigation cannot exist without a prefetch (it's what the reducer acts upon when changing the router state), so that's why we have the concept of a "temporary" prefetch.

I don't think you're mixing the concepts though, `<Link prefetch />` does indeed _mostly_ map to what `prefetchKind` is, with the exception of the temporary one as you've noted. The comments in this file could use updating.

- `PrefetchKind.FULL` = `prefetch={true}`
- `PrefetchKind.AUTO` = prefetch left unspecified, or `prefetch={null}`
- `PrefetchKind.TEMPORARY` = A placeholder for a navigation that occurred without a regular prefetch. For example if you have `prefetch={false}`, or you're in dev, a temporary prefetch is created. If we later discover a prefetch intent, `TEMPORARY` will get replaced with whatever that intent is.

body:
> What are the cases when "loose" might break someone's CSS?

When page 1 imports a.css and b.css in that order and page 2 imports b.css and a.css in that order.

Loose mode would merge that together in any order, assuming there is no dependency between these two css files.

Strict mode would not merge them together and loads them in a -> b on page 1 and b -> a on page 2.

Note that this scenario only makes sense if there is no client side navigation possible between page 1 and page 2, since client side navigation won't change existing stylesheet, so it won't reorder the stylesheets when navigating from page 1 to 2.

body:
Those are the five configured test type values:

```js
[
  new RegExp('^(test/(development|e2e)|packages/.*/src/.*)/.*\\.test\\.(js|jsx|ts|tsx)$'),
  new RegExp('^(test/(production|e2e))/.*\\.test\\.(js|jsx|ts|tsx)$'),
  new RegExp('^test/unit|packages/.*/src/.*/.*\\.test\\.(js|jsx|ts|tsx)$'),
  'examples/',
  'test/integration/',
  'test/e2e/'
]
```

Before this change, we coerced the first two RegExps to a string that never matched. And the three actual strings were prepended with `test/` incorrectly. Now, we use the three string values as-is since the test file might start with those. So we were and are not matching `development` and `production`. Should we?

Side note: This only affects Windows, because in the GitHub Actions we're passing an explicit `--type`, so this logic is not used at all there.

It's needed for the loader to resolve to import JSON with an assertion:

[SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'with']

I think this optimization needs to be removed entirely. We always need to visit statement's children. The other `Analyzer` checks are for `import`/`export` declarations, which are only valid a the top level. If we're checking for `import`/`require` expressions, they can happen anywhere in the tree.

This also probably means that you should do some basic benchmarking here to make sure there's no significant regressions caused by visiting all the AST nodes in the analyzer.

Meaning we only need to visit statements for the new comment functionality (= `comments.is_some()`)?

body:
Yeah the previous implementation would not visit them at all. The new code in `visit_call_expr` only makes sense if we have comments so if the `Analyzer` is not given comment data then checking statements is just wasted CPU since we traverse the entire tree to do nothing.

In practice, the analyzer gets comments now every time since we need to respect these directives in all contexts, which means we do more work here than before. I will try to get some numbers but I don't see a way to support this feature without walking the entire AST.

body:
That does seem like it could be nice in avoiding duplicate lookups of the function, but it looks like `try_start_task_execution` has an implicit dependency on `CURRENT_TASK_STATE`:
- `MemoryBackend::try_start_task_execution` synchronously calls `Task::execute`.
- `Task::execute` synchronously calls `TaskAggregationContext::apply_queued_updates`
- `TaskAggregationContext::apply_queued_updates` synchronously calls `TurboTasks::schedule_notify_tasks_set`
- **`TurboTasks::schedule_notify_tasks_set` modifies `tasks_to_notify` from `CURRENT_TASK_STATE`**

So I can't do this (without significant refactoring) because it would create a circular dependency issue for `CURRENT_TASK_STATE`.

body: That looks a bit inconsitent/weird to me. Why does a LocalOutput need a TaskId and a LocalCell and ExecutionId? A LocalOutput shouldn't escape the current task (similar to LocalCell), so it shouldn't need that.
author: sokra

body:
In theory, since a `LocalOutput` shouldn't be able to escape the current task, this *shouldn't* be needed, but:

- The `ResolvedValue` trait is not infallible, even once it's used everywhere, as there will still be ways to store `Vc`s in global state. Storing `TaskId` here gives us a way to perform additional runtime checks (eventually maybe only in debug mode?).

- Making this check airtight (removing the need for a runtime check) would require adding lifetimes to `Vc` to prevent it from being stored globally, but we decided against that for now.

- These runtime checks are particularly useful in the interim before we're fully migrated to `ResolvedValue` and `ResolvedVc`.

- The short-term plan of storing `LocalOutput` globally to mitigate these escapes and allow us to roll out something sooner requires a `TaskId`: https://www.notion.so/vercel/RawVc-LocalOutput-aede5f463f594ca58396eb3fdaffd865?pvs=4#02af94e3b9b64a3690f3e467abc0a47e

This serves a role similar to `ExecutionId` on `LocalCell`, except that the short-term plan of storing `LocalOutput` globally sadly necessitates using a `TaskId` instead of an `ExecutionId` for now.

Unfortunately, since `CurrentGlobalTaskState` is stored as a `task_local!`, there's no sane way to use the generic `B::TaskState`.

If I made `CurrentGlobalTaskState` generic, I'd need to change the type of `CURRENT_GLOBAL_TASK_STATE` to be `Arc<RwLock<dyn Any>>`, and that would introduce a ton of checked casts (which might be more expensive than the extra `Box` here was in the first place).

IMO the boxing here isn't that bad. The boxing that the `TurboTasksBackendApiExt` APIs must do is more concerning (as that's likely a hotter codepath).

The memory overhead of `CurrentGlobalTaskState` shouldn't matter too much since it's only for actively running tasks, and if it does, the better solution is for us to limit concurrency.

body: It is used to speed up iteration. We sometimes have to iterate e. g. all `Children` of a task and that would require walking the whole map in `Plain` mode. But that is pretty expensive if we have e. g. 3 children, but 5000 dependent tasks. So when we have many entries we switch to Indexed mode which stores entries per type of entry. Technically Indexed is a bit less memory efficient and less performant for single lookups, but much more efficient for iteration.

body:
I think you are right, but would this be better?

With the ordered approach it could hold the smaller lock while waiting for the bigger lock. So some time unnecessary holding a lock.

Example

A wants 3 and 4, B wants 2 and 3 and C wants 1 and 2.

They are executed in order A, B, C all needing to operate for 1ms.

Ordered:
0ms:
A locks 3 and 4 and starts doing something.
B locks 2 and waits for 3 as it's already locked.
C locks 1 and waits for 2 as it's already locked.
1ms:
A unlocks 3 and 4.
B gets 3 and starts doing something.
2ms:
B unlocks 2 and 3.
C gets 2 and starts doing something.
3ms:
C unlocks 1 and 2.
Finished after 3ms.

Current:
0ms:
A locks 3 and 4 and starts doing something.
B locks 2, doesn't get 3, unlocks 2 and waits for 3.
C locks 1 and 2 and starts doing something.
1ms:
A unlocks 3 and 4.
C unlocks 1 and 2.
B gets 3, locks 2 and starts doing something.
2ms:
B unlocks 2 and 3.
FInished after 2ms.

body:
I think you should land this as-is, but...

It might be possible to make the public transaction API safe with zero runtime cost by using `ghost_cell`: https://docs.rs/ghost-cell/latest/ghost_cell/

- `GhostToken` can only be constructed by passing in a closure that receives a `GhostToken<'brand>`. That token cannot escape the closure. That would mean that APIs like `execute_context` would also need to take a closure with an `ExecuteContext<'brand>` instead of returning an `ExecuteContext<'a>` (this somewhat inverts the control flow and may or may not be feasible).

- `'brand` is an invariant lifetime (preventing upcasting/downcasting) via [this trick](https://github.com/matthieu-m/ghost-cell/blob/956df44625bda13793defc4a826431ad9ab7789c/src/ghost_cell.rs#L533). That solves the problems of being able to pass a transaction to the wrong backend.

Here's the full paper if you're interested: https://plv.mpi-sws.org/rustbelt/ghostcell/paper.pdf

> I used some concurrent-queue before in the old backend
> It is not able to atomically pop ALL items

It looks like `MARK_BIT` that `.close()`/`.is_closed` in `concurrent-queue` uses `SeqCst`? https://github.com/smol-rs/concurrent-queue/blob/e874f701f8413de01948c4903f894e5c845d8950/src/unbounded.rs#L391-L402

I think if you close the queue first, [`concurrent_queue::ConcurrentQueue`'s `try_iter` method](https://docs.rs/concurrent-queue/latest/concurrent_queue/struct.ConcurrentQueue.html#method.try_iter) _should_ atomically return all the elements? (Note: `TryIter::next()` is just calling `.pop()`)

If you want to atomically swap out the entire `ConcurrentQueue` for a new one when you do that (so that there's not a closed queue exposed), you could use a `RwLock` around the entire queue (preferably an [eventually fair](https://docs.rs/parking_lot/latest/parking_lot/type.RwLock.html#fairness) one?) or [maybe an `ArcSwap`](https://docs.rs/arc-swap/latest/arc_swap/)?

body:
You should just get this landed, and not block on this. However...

I was thinking about this a bit more, and have some ideas on how (if we want to keep `Sharded`) this might be improved.

Since we don't actually care what shard data ends up in (unlike `DashMap`, which does), we can:
- Pick a random shard, rather than hashing. This is probably a little faster.
- If shard `n` is locked (using `Mutex::try_lock`), just go to the next (`(n+1) % length`) shard, repeated for some limited number of attempts. Don't bother trying to wait to acquire the lock unless we run out of attempts.
- Since lock contention shouldn't matter as much (we can just go to the next shard), decrease the total number of shards.

Another improvement might be to make shards "sticky": Keep a thread local of the last shard id we used, and try re-using that first before picking a random shard. In the steady-state, as long as there are more shards than threads, each thread will end up with one shard that it "owns".

What I believe to be happening is with webpack when it's false there is still _some_ instability, but it is following each first tree reference deeply, seeing those stylesheets, adding them, and climbing back to the initial file and adding those stylesheets.

When only stylesheets are being included in side effects, the JS tree climbing is being ignored and the CSS files are being added in order that they are run into (top of tree to bottom, a complete inversion and broken behavior). When true, the CSS files are added according to the JS tree from bottom to top in full library order, rather than semi-random order like false.

body:
FYI rehashing/double-hashing shouldn't really have any advantages here over simpler linear probing (using `(trimmed_hash + 1) % digit_mask`), as long as you have a high quality hash function (which xxh3 is):

- Hashes are displaced either way, whether it's a rehashed version or a `+1` version, the end result is basically the same
- A quality hash function should start you at a "random" position each time, so linear probing shouldn't introduce any higher risk of collision with hashes that come after it.

The advantages of double hashing are increased resistance to collisions when using weak hash functions or dealing with pathological inputs: https://stackoverflow.com/a/29641558

Okay if you want to leave it this way with double hashing because it feels "safer" or because "that's how webpack does it".

body:
(More broadly than just this PR) I don't know all the places `Vc<ModuleId>` is used, but we should probably avoid storing collections of `ModuleId`s as a bunch of tiny `Vc`s, and just store and pass them [around by value](https://turbopack-rust-docs.vercel.sh/rustdoc/turbo_tasks/struct.Value.html#impl-TaskInput-for-Value%3CT%3E) in most cases.

A `ModuleId` is

```
#[turbo_tasks::value(shared)]
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Hash, Ord, PartialOrd, DeterministicHash)]
#[serde(untagged)]
pub enum ModuleId {
    Number(u64),
    String(RcStr),
}
```

which is 16 bytes (and could be 8 bits if `Number` was `NonZeroU64`, thanks to the niche optimization!). A `Vc` is also 16 bytes (plus all the overhead of allocating a cell in the backend for it, if it wasn't already in a cell).

body:
Keep in mind that we are working with a very short hash, so conflicts are likely.

> * Hashes are displaced either way, whether it's a rehashed version or a `+1` version, the end result is basically the same

It matters when you end up having 3 or more conflicts on the same slot. And also when them number of conflicts changes.

An example: Let's assume `a`, `b`, `c` and `d` all end up on the same slot on the first hashing.

Scenario: Start with `a, c, d` on first compilation and add `b`

Initial:

```
Module  Linear    Rehashing
a       slot      slot
c       slot +1   hash2(c) slot
d       slot +2   hash2(d) slot
```

After change:

```
Module  Linear    Rehashing
a       slot      slot
b       slot +1   hash2(b) slot
c       slot +2   hash2(c) slot
d       slot +3   hash2(d) slot
```

So the linear approach causes `c` and `d` to have their module id unneeded changed, while the rehashing avoid that in that case. Assuming no follow up conflict, the maximum number of changed module ids is 2 in the rehashing approach and N in the linear approach, where N is the number of modules conflicting on that initial slot.

So I would prefer the rehashing

body:
This is an example of a complicated change that seems intractable/impractical to solve with AST-based codemods.

- I needed to add `.to_resolved().await?` to the result of `path.join(...)` to convert it from a `Vc` to a `ResolvedVc`, but:
- This code is inside of a call to [`Iterator::map`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.map).
- `map` takes a synchronous closure. There's no easy way to call an async function inside of `map`.
- I had to convert the `.map()` to a for loop, and replace the call to [`Iterator::collect`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.collect) with code that construct an `AutoMap` and then `insert`s into it.
- I had to use Rust-Analyzer (via LSP in my editor) to check the type signature of `DirectoryContent::new` to see that it expects `AutoMap`, because that's not obvious within the context of this code.
- I had to use Rust-Analyzer to auto-insert the import for `AutoMap`, using it's first suggestion.

This might be solvable with an LLM that knows how to use tools (the LSP).
author: bgw

body:
The `normalize` closure here isn't something I'd expect a codemod to do, I just decided to clean this up a bit while I was here.

I'd expect a codemod to just put the `.to_resolved().await?` inline.

However, this is another example of a case where I had to eliminate `Iterator::map` and `Iterator::collect` calls.
author: bgw

body:
This code was a bit whacky. It was calling `Vc::cell(...).resolve().await`, which doesn't make much sense because a newly constructed `Vc` is always resolved...

Cleaned this up a bit since I was here, but this isn't something I'd expect a codemod to do.

I wasn't able to find this antipattern anywhere else in our codebase (checked with astgrep).

body: Should we make the public signature of turbo-tasks functions take `impl Into<Vc<...>>` instead of `Vc<...>`, so one can pass Vc and ResolvedVc (and VcOperation)?
author: sokra

body:
That's an interesting idea that I haven't considered. I'm going to be conservative and say "no" for now because:

- This deref is probably the easiest thing for me to codemod. In most cases the compiler can auto-suggest the exact change needed.
- Making the functions generic might have a slight negative impact on code size and compile times.
- This more complicated signature might make the rustdocs harder to read?

But if the derefs end up being annoying to people (added syntactic noise), we can do this.

Regarding "magic" in API (and especially macro) design: I'd like to keep it to a minimum. I didn't really like the change I had to do to let functions accept `ResolvedVc` exposed as `Vc` types, but I had to do it because the consequences of not doing that were far worse.

This test was recently added in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/70446 but it makes an incorrect assumption about client router cache invalidation.

It was working previously because we weren't honoring the static staletime for the static page, but since the fix in this PR, it now respects the static staletime. And as described in the [docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/caching#invalidation-1), you'd need to have called a `revalidate` API in a server action to simultaneously clear the client router cache. 

My changes here refresh the page so the client router cache will be invalidated. The underlying test is still preserved since a refresh would have seeded the same stale data if it didn't handle the revalidation.

body:
This seems like the worst offense here? This is an `RcStr`. We shouldn't convert it into a `String` until the very last minute.

Since every piece of the source string can be represented by a `&str` (all of which are `'static` except this one), the most efficient thing to do might be to build a `SmallVec<[&str, 7]>`, turning it into a `String` (using `std::slice::join`) only at the end.

That way, the `String` [can know *exactly* how many bytes to allocate (guaranteed limit of 1 allocation)](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f4966590d8edd5f493a1aab04016b94a75494329/library/alloc/src/str.rs#L145-L157), and if we need to insert at the beginning of `SmallVec`, it's a cheaper `memmove` of a few pointers, as opposed to a potentially long string of bytes.

If this code is an extremely hot path, there's more we could do to remove the need for `SmallVec` as well, but I'm guessing it's not worth it.

body:
Hmm... I wonder if statically optimizable GET handlers need to be annotated at build time to run in `'render'` phase always even when triggered dynamically. And all other GET handlers need to be annotated at build time to run in `'action'` phase. It's odd that a route handler could not set cookies during prerender but then if you happened to hit the route handler dynamically it would allow cookies to be set, but if the handler became static again it would again disallow handlers.

By testing the route for whether it is statically optimizable at build time we can discover whether the handler adheres to render phase semantics. If it does we should run it with those semantics all the time even if we happen to trigger it dynamically. And if we can't statically optimize it we assume it has action semantics and always consistently run it with those.

Not sure if routes can even be hit dynamically when they are statically optimized so maybe this is a moot point but the invariant I think we need to hold to is we don't use one phase during prerenders and another during dynamic renders for the same handler

body:
Debug builds will panic on arithmetic overflow, so the subtraction part is fine, but for the `as u32` (which will never panic on overflow):

- If this is part of a hot loop, this should at least have a `debug_assert!` to check the cast.
- If this isn't part of a hot loop, this should use `u32::try_from(children.len()).unwrap()`.

I think the lack of panicking behavior on `as` casts was a language design mistake, [but unfortunately it's too late to reasonably add that to the language](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/rust-2018-facing-the-cast-problem/8328/3).

```suggestion
        // `$task` might be a `TaskGuard` type, in which case, `.get()` might call `TaskGuard::get`
        #[allow(unused_imports)]
        use $crate::backend::operation::TaskGuard as _;
```

You don't need to copy the comment everywhere, but the `as _` should be copied for all of these macros. It's just there to avoid any unnecessary shadowing of the `TaskGuard` name in the macro.

If you *know* for certain that `$task` is always a `TaskGuard`, you should probably remove the import and just replace the method call with `$crate::backend::operation::TaskGuard::get($task)` instead. Performing method resolution inside macros can have unexpected results.

body:
If we extend the cache entries we end up with different hidden classes in the code when more than one cache handler is active which would cause that code to deopt, thrash the JIT and eventually stable out in a sub-optimal polymorphic state.

It's better that we compose them instead. (Also just composition > inheritance in general.)

For example:

```
type DefaultCacheEntry = {
  entry: CacheEntry,
  isErrored: boolean
  errorRetryCount: number
  size?: number
}
```

This also makes it clearer which are internals of this and never could possibly leak outside the implementation of the cache handler into the implementation of use-cache-wrapper.

body:
```suggestion
If you want the current time to represent the time of a user Request, add `await connection()` before you read the current time. This instructs Next.js that everything after the `await connection()` requires there to be a user Request before it can run. If you add `await connection()` you will also need to ensure there is a Suspense boundary somewhere above the waiting component that describes a fallback UI React can use. The Suspense can be anywhere in the parent component stack but it is shown here above the waiting component for demonstration purposes.
```

body:
Thanks for the comment! I'll pull the note out so that it's not duplicated.

As for this being a generic warning that applies to any API, I think I respectfully disagree. In my experience, there are a lot of APIs that are designed to accept untrusted user input. For example, `React.createElement` escapes strings to avoid XSS specifically so that you can display untrusted user input. As another example, the browser API that is closest to `router.push`, `history.pushState`, is not susceptible to XSS URLs and can accept untrusted user input, as far as I understand.

Also, as I noted in the original bug report, with minimal searching I found over 1,000 public projects on Github that are probably vulnerable to this problem, and that is certainly an undercount, as I only looked for ones that called their user variable `callbackUrl`. So even if this is generic advice, it seems like developers are not understanding that it needs to be followed in this particular instance.

body:
I spent some time bashing my head against the wall wondering if this could be rewritten as a two `BTreeMap`s, one of start, and one of end points.

But I realized the issue: Two `BTreeMap`s could find any range that's a subset of your lookup range, but there's no efficient way to get a range that's a superset of your lookup range.

All the rangeset/rangemap implementations seem to be coalescing too, which makes none of them viable for this use-case. 😞 

... So this tree-based implementation makes sense to me, even if I'm a bit upset that we have to maintain this rather complicated code.

body:
This whole "write rows to a vec" thing makes sense if one of the following is true:

1. You desperately need to reduce the time you hold the store write lock open and can't wait for de-serialization to happen.
2. You don't want partial writes to the store to happen in the case of a deserialization failure.

Number 1 seems like it shouldn't matter because deserialization should be fast. Number 2 might matter, but we can probably assume that deserialization doesn't fail and panic if it does?

If one of those two isn't true, you could call `self.process` inside the deserialization loop, and remove the need for a vec entirely.

`package_json_path` is now a `&ResolvedVc<FileSystemPath>`. The first deref is used to get a `ResolvedVc<FileSystemPath>`. The second deref is used to get a `Vc<FileSystemPath>`.

`&ResolvedVc` doesn't make sense if you can avoid it, because `ResolvedVc` is `Copy`, but it's not always easy to avoid. In this case, it's because `package_json_context` is a `ReadRef`, which only gives a reference to the underlying data.

body:
```suggestion
By default, any data accessed during render is treated as if it should be evaluated at request time. To explicitly communicate to Next.js that some data should be prerenderable, you must explicitly cache it using `"use cache"` or `unstable_cache`.
```
author: delbaoliveira

body:
```suggestion
However, you may have taken great care to have a fully or partially prerenderable route and it would be quite easy to accidentally make such a route non-prerenderable by introducing a new data dependency you forgot to cache. To prevent this, Next.js requires that data accessed without caching must be inside a Suspense boundary that defines a fallback UI to use while loading this data.
```
author: delbaoliveira

body:
```suggestion
This makes React's `Suspense` component an explicit opt-in to allow uncached data access.
```
author: delbaoliveira

body:
```suggestion
To ensure you have a fully prerenderable route, you should omit any Suspense boundaries in your route. Suspense is useful for loading UI dynamically but if you have entirely prerenderable pages there is no need to have fallback UI because the primary UI will always be available.
```
author: delbaoliveira

body:
```suggestion
To allow uncached data anywhere in your application, you can add a Suspense boundary just inside your `<body>` tag in your Root Layout. However, we don't recommend you do this because you will likely want to scope Suspense boundaries around more granular component boundaries that provide fallback UI specific to individual Components.
```
author: delbaoliveira

body:
```suggestion
Hybrid applications will typically use a combination of both techniques, with your top level shared Layouts being prerendered for static pages (without Suspense), and your layouts that actually have data dependencies defining fallback UI.
```
author: delbaoliveira

If your application needs to read cookies the only recourse you have is to opt into allowing this data read using `Suspense`.
```

body: Just one informational Q about explicit derefs that didn't have to occur when using normal Vcs. Otherwise ✔️
author: arlyon

body:
Rust's autoderef rules are [for receiver arguments (`self`) on method calls](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html). It doesn't apply to normal arguments of function calls. ☹️

`emit_with_completion` is a `#[turbo_tasks::function]`, so it accepts a `Vc` argument, and not a `ResolvedVc` argument, even if the underlying function is written using `ResolvedVc` (as per the [signature rewrite rules](https://turbopack-rust-docs.vercel.sh/turbo-engine/tasks.html#external-signature-rewriting)).

We could avoid this by making `Vc` arguments generic (e.g. `impl Into<Vc<Foo>>`), but:

- That would have pretty negative implications for compilation time by introducing lots of monomorphization.
- Generics make type inference less useful. We rely on inference for most calls to `Vc::cell` for transparent value types, and if the argument type is a generic, Rust can't infer what the return type should be. So you'd need to rewrite `my_turbo_task_func(Vc::cell(arg))` as `my_turbo_task_func(Vc::cell::<ExplicitType>(arg))`.

body:
> Why can't we find sourcemaps for these URLs?

The common scenario is that the frame is from our bundled runtimes. These are required as externals and have `webpack://` frames. Since they are external, Turbopack doesn't know about these frames. We special cased it here, but are missing the same check in `createOriginalStackFrame`. 

However, this only works for externals that are Webpack bundles. We can have a lot more externals configured though and they might just be regular file frames or frames from another bundler.

So we should either always start with native and fallback to bundler or only fallback to native when the bundler throws. Seems like it's mostly a perf question.

body: I've been investigating a Next.js bug that intersects with this PR. The basic setup is: ```jsx export default async function Page() { 'use cache' cacheLife({ revalidate: 0 }) // OR cacheLife({ expire: 299 }) const data = await fetch(...) return <>... } ``` That triggers the ["A component accessed data, headers, params, searchParams, or a short-lived cache without a Suspense boundary nor a "use cache" above it" error](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/a44a0d91b2038d16c3b1c51f1d339d54e87aa9c1/packages/next/src/server/app-render/dynamic-rendering.ts#L606) due to [skipping the static render for those `cacheLife` configurations](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/a44a0d91b2038d16c3b1c51f1d339d54e87aa9c1/packages/next/src/server/use-cache/use-cache-wrapper.ts#L536-L549). Prior to this PR, the error was created by the `trackAllowedDynamicAccess` call for `firstAttemptServerController`: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/a44a0d91b2038d16c3b1c51f1d339d54e87aa9c1/packages/next/src/server/app-render/app-render.tsx#L2109-L2120 However, this PR modifies that `onError` function to ignore when `initialServerPrerenderController.signal.aborted || initialServerRenderController.signal.aborted`: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/0f176bbe807151674189883269d770f05ee659bd/packages/next/src/server/app-render/app-render.tsx#L2012-L2020 After this PR, the error is now created by (one of) the `trackAllowedDynamicAccess` call(s) for `finalClientController`: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/0f176bbe807151674189883269d770f05ee659bd/packages/next/src/server/app-render/app-render.tsx#L2194-L2202 And I see that this PR ignores `finalServerController.signal.aborted` unless `isPrerenderInterruptedError(err)`: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/0f176bbe807151674189883269d770f05ee659bd/packages/next/src/server/app-render/app-render.tsx#L2161-L2166 So I am wondering: should the `onError` conditional for `finalClientController` check `isPrerenderInterruptedError(err) && finalClientController.signal.aborted` instead of `isPrerenderInterruptedError(err) || finalClientController.signal.aborted`? Also, as an aside, why is a server component triggering an error in conjunction with finalClientController? (I apologize if these are a dumb questions; this is my first deep dive into Next.js internals. 😅)
author: jonathanhefner

body:
thanks for reaching out. You've stumbled upon a heuristic we need to document better and figure out how to clarify in the error messages but I believe things are working as intended. When we prerender we are seeing if the route can render without any non-determinism. Basically we try to produce an HTML page that is suitable to server to any visitor. So how do we know what is deterministic? Without caching basically everything is dynamic except literally static stuff like ``` export default async function Page() { return
This page is 100% static, it's all in the code!
} ``` So that's coherent but not super useful b/c then only very trivial routes could ever be prerendered. So we say that in addition to static things we can also include things we know how to cache. But there is a catch. If we cache the thing that's great but if you tell me the cache is only good for 1 hour then I need to remember to prerender that page again in 1 hour b/c the "non-determinism" of the cache entry is only valid for that time period. So then we get to the heuristic. If you tell me that you want to cache something so it can be prerendered but you also tell me it will expire in under 5 minutes we make the decision to say that even though we *could* include it in the prerender we're going to not do that. With such a short expiration time unless you have very frequent traffic to that page it'll often be expired and need to do a dynamic render anyway so the prerendering is sort of pointless. So from a prerendering perspective caches with very short lifetimes are "dynamic" and excluded from prerenders and thus you need a Suspense boundary above that short-lived cache which is what this error is telling you. The other heuristic we use is if you set the revaldiate to zero we also consider that cache dynamic for purposes of prerendering. I'm less familiar with the history here but I think we have treated reavlidate: 0 as a dynamic and we're sort of adopting that heurstic here. IMO though we probably shouldn't because revalidate: 0 and revalidate: 0.001 should probably have basically the same behavior and right now I don't think they do. But back to your feedback about isPrerenderInterruptedError. This is really for when you do something like read Math.random() outside of a cache. This currently can show up in the SSR render even if the SSR render itself hasn't aborted yet so that's why we check for both independently (|| not &&) as for >Also, as an aside, why is a server component triggering an error in conjunction with finalClientController? In this context server refers to RSC or the `react-server` condition. Conceptually you can imagine we render the RSC output in a node process with `react-server` condition which causes certain module to be loaded over others And client refers to SSR or the absence of `react-server` condition. Conceptually you can imagine that this is a render of HTML receiving the RSC output from the other process and this process is spawned without the `react-server` condition which causes different module implementations to be loaded. In the world of RSC, server components are server and client components are client. BUT when you SSR you are rendering "the client" on the server. So that's why I'm calling it a client controller. I could say SSR controller too but I just didn't.

body:
Thank you for the detailed explanation!

> If you tell me that you want to cache something so it can be prerendered but you also tell me it will expire in under 5 minutes we make the decision to say that even though we _could_ include it in the prerender we're going to not do that. With such a short expiration time unless you have very frequent traffic to that page it'll often be expired and need to do a dynamic render anyway so the prerendering is sort of pointless. So from a prerendering perspective caches with very short lifetimes are "dynamic" and excluded from prerenders and thus you need a Suspense boundary above that short-lived cache which is what this error is telling you.

From an engineering perspective, the behavior does make sense — Next.js is essentially protecting you from yourself.  However, from a user / DX perspective, it feels like a point of friction.  Even with an improved error message, it would be somewhat frustrating to suddenly have to add a `Suspense` wrapper just because you switched from `cacheLife('minutes')` to `cacheLife('seconds')`.

It's kind of like I, as an app developer, have entered into an agreement with Next.js, wherein I add `'use cache'` + revalidation as appropriate, and in exchange I get improved performance and everything works.  But then Next.js suddenly decides to do extra work that I didn't agree to, and demands payment (a `Suspense` boundary) in return.  It's an infringement of the agreement.

Would it be possible for Next.js to automatically insert a `Suspense` boundary when it performs this specific optimization?  (I would guess that automatic `Suspense` boundaries have been discussed and rejected because it's too complex to determine optimal placement, but, for this specific case, there is a compelling argument for the obvious spot.)

> And client refers to SSR or the absence of `react-server` condition. Conceptually you can imagine that this is a render of HTML receiving the RSC output from the other process and this process is spawned without the `react-server` condition which causes different module implementations to be loaded.
>
> In the world of RSC, server components are server and client components are client. BUT when you SSR you are rendering "the client" on the server. So that's why I'm calling it a client controller. I could say SSR controller too but I just didn't.

If I understand correctly, you are saying: client components are prerendered (which is done on the server), and because client components can interleave server components, the client component renderer needs the output of the server component renderer.  Is that correct?

If so, I'm still unclear about why `finalClientController` triggers an error that is specific to a server component.  The location of the error makes it seem like the client rendering process itself is attempting to render the server component.  Shouldn't the server component be rendered (or marked as dynamically rendered) by that point?

(By the way, if you prefer, I can move all of this to a Discussion post so I don't bog down your PR.)
